Case_Content:
Man, 64 years old, no significant medical history, presenting with a left colon tumor revealed by subocclusive syndrome.  Thoraco-abdominal CT scan shows a 6 cm colonic mass and two liver metastases in segments II and V measuring 2.2 and 3 cm. CEA: 120 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, MSS. No extra-hepatic disease.
MDT Discussion: Metastases considered primarily resectable, symptomatic colonic lesion is the priority.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Resectable  
- Justification:  
  • Only two liver metastases (2.2 cm in segment II, 3 cm in segment V), both ≤5 cm and limited to two segments.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease on CT.  
  • No reported vascular, biliary or portal invasion; thus technically amenable to complete (R0) resection while preserving at least two contiguous liver segments.  
  • Patient is 64 y, with no significant comorbidities reported, suggesting adequate physiologic reserve to tolerate liver surgery.  
  • Primary tumor is symptomatic (obstruction) and therefore also requires resection; the combined disease burden is low enough to allow either simultaneous or staged approach.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Urgent resection of the left‑sided primary tumor (segmental colectomy with primary anastomosis or diverting stoma if intra‑operative assessment deems anastomosis unsafe).  
   – Rationale: obstruction is the immediate clinical priority; removal of the primary eliminates the source of sepsis and allows subsequent systemic therapy.  

B. Intra‑operative assessment of hepatic reserve (volumetric CT or intra‑operative ultrasound). If future liver remnant (FLR) is estimated ≥30 % of total liver volume and vascular inflow/outflow can be preserved, proceed with simultaneous limited hepatic resection (wedge resection of segment II lesion and segmentectomy of segment V lesion).  
   – Rationale: both lesions are small, located in separate lobes, and can be removed with a minor hepatectomy; simultaneous surgery shortens overall treatment time and avoids a second major operation.  

C. If FLR is insufficient or operative conditions are unfavorable, adopt a staged approach:  
   1. Complete colon resection first (as in A).  
   2. Allow 4–6 weeks recovery, then perform liver resection (either anatomical segmentectomy or parenchymal‑sparing wedge resections) after reassessment of FLR.  
   – Rationale: ensures patient safety while still achieving curative intent.  

D. Adjuvant systemic therapy (post‑operative, 6 months): FOLFOX (5‑FU/leucovorin/oxaliplatin) ± anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab) given RAS‑wild‑type status.  
   – Rationale: improves disease‑free survival and addresses occult micrometastatic disease.  

E. Surveillance: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced CT of chest/abdomen every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually, with MRI liver if any equivocal findings.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient has a single 2.5 cm peripheral metastasis in segment VI, no radiologically evident extra hepatic disease, and the lesion is amenable to a non anatomic wedge resection with an expected R0 margin. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered to be resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial anatomy. Precise anatomic mapping is required to avoid intra operative surprise.

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) because the tumor is KRAS mutated (no anti EGFR benefit).
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver MRI (and contrast-enhanced CT).

C. Surgical management
• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a simultaneous right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + a segment VI wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. (Simultaneous resection for solitary peripheral metastases is safe and oncologically equivalent to staged procedures.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
• Alternative : consider two-stage surgical resection of primary and liver tumors / consider right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + an image-guided ablation using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals. A level of 35 ng/mL is acceptable but warrants close surveillance (Minagawa et al.)

Case_Content:
Woman, 56 years old, incidental discovery of a right colon tumor during a workup for iron deficiency anemia. Thoraco-Abdominal CT scan shows an ileocecal mass and a single 2.5 cm metastasis in segment VI. CEA 35 ng/mL, KRAS mutation present. No other lesions on FDG-PET.
MDT Discussion: Single peripheral metastasis, situation suitable for combined surgical treatment.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- The patient has a single peripheral liver metastasis measuring 2.5 cm in segment VI, no vascular or biliary invasion reported, and no extra‑hepatic disease on PET‑CT.  
- Current oncologic criteria define resectability as the ability to achieve an R0 resection of all disease while preserving at least two contiguous liver segments with adequate inflow, outflow and a future liver remnant (FLR) >30 % in normal liver.  
- Resection of a solitary sub‑segmental lesion in segment VI would leave the majority of the liver intact; the expected FLR is well above the safety threshold.  
- Therefore, the disease is resectable (not merely potentially resectable) according to standard hepatobiliary oncology guidelines.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive pre‑operative work‑up  
   - Obtain a contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or gadoxetate‑enhanced MRI) to confirm lesion size, exact location, relationship to hepatic vessels, and to exclude occult lesions.  
   - Perform colonoscopy with biopsy if not already done, and stage the primary tumor (T/N status, differentiation).  
   - Assess patient fitness (ECOG/ASA, cardiopulmonary reserve, liver function tests) and calculate FLR volume (CT‑based volumetry).  

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (optional but recommended)  
   - Because the metastasis is technically resectable but the primary tumor is still in situ, give 3–4 cycles of a fluoropyrimidine‑oxaliplatin doublet (e.g., mFOLFOX6) plus a VEGF‑targeted agent (bevacizumab) – anti‑EGFR agents are ineffective with KRAS mutation.  
   - Rationale: peri‑operative chemotherapy improves disease‑free survival, allows assessment of tumor biology, and may down‑size the lesion further, facilitating a margin‑negative liver resection.  

C. Surgical phase – Simultaneous (combined) resection  
   - Perform a right hemicolectomy (ileocecal resection with adequate lymphadenectomy) together with a segment VI wedge/segmentectomy or non‑anatomical resection of the metastasis.  
   - Rationale: the primary tumor is asymptomatic, the liver lesion is peripheral and small, and combined surgery avoids a second operation, shortens overall treatment time, and is supported by the MDT’s statement that the situation is suitable for combined surgical treatment.  

D. Post‑operative management  
   - Resume systemic chemotherapy (completion of 6 months total, including pre‑operative cycles) with the same regimen used pre‑operatively, adjusted for postoperative recovery.  
   - Monitor CEA and perform surveillance imaging (CT or MRI of liver, chest CT) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  
   - Provide standard postoperative care (DVT prophylaxis, early mobilization, nutritional support) and assess for any complications (Clavien‑Dindo grading).

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, history of smoking, presenting with T3N1 upper rectal adenocarcinoma with a single 1.8 cm liver metastasis in segment III. Pelvic MRI: limited parietal invasion. CEA 45 ng/mL. RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Single resectable metastasis, possibility of coordinated surgical treatment after short-course radiotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
The patient is potentially resectable.  
Justification:  
- Liver disease: solitary metastasis, 1.8 cm, located in segment III (peripheral left‑lateral sector), which is amenable to a non‑anatomic wedge or segmentectomy while preserving ≥2 contiguous segments of functional liver.  
- No reported vascular or biliary involvement, and the lesion size is well below the usual 5 cm threshold that predicts technical difficulty.  
- No extra‑hepatic disease has been documented, but thoraco‑abdominal imaging has not been performed, so the absence of distant metastases cannot be confirmed.  
- The primary rectal tumor is T3N1, asymptomatic, and will receive short‑course radiotherapy; it does not currently mandate emergent resection.  
Because definitive staging (CT chest/abdomen, liver MRI, assessment of future liver remnant volume) is missing, the case cannot be declared outright resectable; it remains potentially resectable pending completion of staging.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Short‑course radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) to the rectum – to achieve local control and allow safe timing of abdominal surgery.  
B. Comprehensive restaging (contrast‑enhanced CT of chest and abdomen, liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast, and calculation of FLR volume). This will confirm absence of extra‑hepatic disease, verify that the segment III lesion is still resectable, and ensure an adequate liver remnant (>30 % in a normal liver, >40 % if steatosis or chemotherapy‑associated injury is suspected).  
C. Surgical phase – if restaging confirms resectability:  
   • Perform a simultaneous minimally invasive approach: laparoscopic low anterior resection (TME) with a protective loop ileostomy, combined with laparoscopic wedge/segment III resection of the liver metastasis. The minor liver resection (<3 segments) and the rectal resection can be safely done in one operative session, minimizing overall hospital stay and preserving oncologic timing.  
   • If intra‑operative findings reveal insufficient FLR or unexpected disease, convert to a staged (liver‑first) approach, completing the liver resection first and delaying the rectal operation.  
D. Adjuvant systemic therapy – postoperative FOLFOX (or CAPOX) for 6 months, with addition of anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab) given RAS wild‑type status, to address micrometastatic disease and reduce recurrence risk.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single 1.8 cm liver metastasis located in segment III, without evidence of extrahepatic disease. The lesion seems technically amenable to a parenchymal-sparing resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for solitary, small metastases, this pattern is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial liver anatomy. 

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab or cetuximab)
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy depending on MDT strategy.
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver and rectum MRI (and contrast-enhanced CT) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control for both

C. Management of the rectal primary (oncologic priority)
• Given the T3N1 upper rectal tumor with limited parietal invasion, long-course radiotherapy is appropriate to optimize local control and allow coordinated surgical planning.

D. Coordinated surgical strategy
• Initiate doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX) during the waiting period following radiotherapy. This period treats potential micrometastatic disease and tests tumor biology.
• Consider image-guided ablation of the single segment III lesion using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)
• After restaging with high-resolution liver MRI and pelvic imaging,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : resection / ablation of the segment III metastasis with follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : resection / ablation of the segment III metastasis followed with strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : liver-first resection or ablation of the single segment III metastasis, then rectal resection after appropriate recovery, using a staged or synchronous strategy : oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
– Parenchymal-sparing segment III wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins.
(Simultaneous resection for solitary peripheral metastases is safe and oncologically equivalent to staged procedures
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Case_Content:
Woman, 72 years old, discovery at abdominal CT scan of a transverse colon adenocarcinoma, CEA 410 ng/mL, three liver metastases (segments IV, V and VI) measuring 2 to 3 cm. Liver MRI: partial contact with the right portal branch without invasion. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Primarily resectable metastases, simple liver surgery possible.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Resectable (upfront resectable).  
- Justification:  
  • Number of liver metastases = 3 (≤ 4 lesions, within commonly accepted limits).  
  • Maximum diameter = 3 cm (≤ 5 cm, favorable for margin‑negative resection).  
  • Anatomical distribution (segments IV, V, VI) allows a non‑major hepatectomy or combined segmental resections while preserving ≥ 2 contiguous segments.  
  • Imaging shows only partial contact with the right portal branch and no definite vascular invasion, making a negative margin technically achievable.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease has been reported on the available scans.  
  • KRAS mutation and BRAF wild‑type do not preclude surgery; BRAF wild‑type is a favorable molecular factor.  
  • MDT comment “simple liver surgery possible” supports technical feasibility.  
  • Assuming adequate liver function and sufficient future liver remnant (FLR) – a prerequisite that has not been contradicted by the data – the case meets current oncologic and technical criteria for resection.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive baseline assessment  
   – Obtain performance status (ECOG/ASA), full comorbidity profile, liver function tests, and calculate FLR (CT volumetry).  
   – Perform thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic metastases.  
   – Record primary‑tumor stage (T, N), grade, and any obstructive/bleeding symptoms.  
   Rationale: confirms patient fitness, ensures no occult disease, and verifies that the FLR is adequate (> 30 % in chemo‑naïve patients, > 40 % after chemotherapy).  

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (peri‑operative chemotherapy)  
   – Regimen: 3 months of oxaliplatin‑based doublet (e.g., FOLFOX) combined with bevacizumab (anti‑VEGF) because KRAS is mutated (anti‑EGFR agents would be ineffective).  
   – Goals: (1) test tumor biology (“proof of time”), (2) potentially down‑size lesions, (3) treat micrometastatic disease, (4) lower postoperative recurrence risk given high CEA (410 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation.  
   – Monitor toxicity and liver function closely.  

C. Restaging after chemotherapy  
   – Repeat liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast and triphasic CT of the chest/abdomen.  
   – Re‑assess lesion size, vascular relationship, and FLR (accounting for any chemotherapy‑induced liver injury).  
   – Confirm that all disease remains resectable and that no new extra‑hepatic sites have appeared.  

D. Surgical resection  
   – If restaging confirms resectability and patient remains fit, proceed to curative‑intent surgery.  
   – Preferred approach: simultaneous resection of the transverse colon primary (segmental colectomy) and liver metastases (segmental/segmentectomy of IV, V, VI) because the liver operation is limited and the primary is asymptomatic.  
   – Alternative (if intra‑operative complexity or patient condition warrants): staged “liver‑first” resection followed by colorectal resection after recovery.  
   – Aim for R0 margins (≥ 1 mm) and preservation of ≥ 2 contiguous liver segments with adequate inflow/outflow.  

E. Adjuvant therapy  
   – Resume/complete systemic chemotherapy (total 6 months peri‑operative) after postoperative recovery, tailored to tolerance.  
   – Consider enrolment in a clinical trial if available (e.g., adjuvant immunotherapy for MSI‑high tumors, though MSI status is unknown).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with three liver metastases located in segments IV, V, and VI (2–3 cm), confined to the right liver and central segments. MRI shows only partial contact with the right portal branch and no evidence of vascular invasion. These lesions appear technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections or anatomicalm resection while preserving adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number and size of metastases with preserved vascular structures, this pattern is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative systemic therapy (strongly recommended)
• The very high CEA level (410 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation suggest biologically aggressive disease.
• Given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control according to patient tolerance.
• This allows treatment of potential micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology before surgery.

B. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of the lesions to the right portal branch and confirm maintained resectability.
• Evaluate future liver remnant (FLR) if right hepatectomy of considered.

C. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform combined parenchymal-sparing resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segment IV wedge/segmentectomy.
– Segment V and VI wedge resections.
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Management of the primary tumor
• Transverse colectomy of extended right colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL).

Case_Content:
Man, 59 years old, T3N1 sigmoid colon tumor associated with four peripheral liver metastases (segments II, III, V, VIII) at the abdominal CT scan. Maximum size: 2.9 cm. CEA 200 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, HER2 negative.
MDT Discussion: Primarily resectable lesions, no vascular or extra-hepatic involvement.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
• The patient has four peripheral liver metastases (segments II, III, V, VIII) each ≤ 3 cm, no vascular or biliary invasion, and no radiologically evident extra‑hepatic disease.  
• Technical criteria for hepatic resection are satisfied: (1) all lesions are amenable to non‑anatomic, parenchymal‑sparing resections; (2) at least two contiguous segments (e.g., I + IV) can be preserved; (3) vascular inflow/outflow and biliary drainage to the future liver remnant (FLR) will be maintained; (4) assuming a normal liver, the anticipated FLR after removal of the four segments would exceed the minimum 30 % functional volume required for a healthy liver.  
• Oncologic criteria are also met: R0 resection appears feasible, the disease is limited to the liver, and the primary tumor is resectable.  

Classification: Resectable (potentially curative) according to current hepatobiliary oncologic standards.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (3 months FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody given RAS‑wild type).  
   – Rationale: high pre‑operative CEA (200 ng/mL) and N1 nodal disease suggest aggressive biology; peri‑operative chemotherapy improves disease‑free survival and provides an in‑vivo test of tumor biology.  

B. Surgical resection of the primary colorectal tumor (sigmoidectomy).  
   – Rationale: removal of the primary eliminates the source of potential obstruction/bleeding and allows definitive pathology (grade, margins, lymphovascular invasion). Timing can be simultaneous with liver surgery if the patient’s physiologic status permits; otherwise, perform after neoadjuvant chemotherapy and before liver resection (primary‑first strategy).  

C. Parenchymal‑sparing liver resection (segmental/wedge resections of segments II, III, V, VIII) after completion of neoadjuvant chemotherapy and confirmation of stable disease on imaging.  
   – Rationale: preserves maximal FLR, avoids major hepatectomy, and achieves R0 margins given the peripheral location of the lesions. Intra‑operative ultrasound should be used to confirm lesion disappearance or residual disease.  

D. Adjuvant systemic therapy (completion of a total of 6 months peri‑operative chemotherapy).  
   – Rationale: consolidates response, addresses micrometastatic disease, and aligns with guideline‑based treatment for synchronous resectable CRLM.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four peripheral liver metastases (segments II, III, V, and VIII), all smaller than 3 cm, without vascular involvement or extrahepatic disease. The distribution is bilobar but the lesions are technically amenable to multiple parenchymal-sparing resections while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number, small size, and peripheral location of metastases, this pattern is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative systemic therapy (recommended)
• The elevated CEA level (200 ng/mL) and multiplicity of lesions suggest biologically active disease.
• Given the high CEA level (200 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI).
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy according to MDT decision.
• This period treats micrometastatic disease and evaluates tumor biology.

B. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

C. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform multiple wedge/segmental resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segments II–III resections (left lateral section wedges).
– Segment V wedge resection.
– Segment VIII wedge resection.
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Management of the primary tumor
• If the sigmoid tumor has not yet been resected, a simultaneous sigmoid colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis can be considered, provided the patient’s condition allows combined surgery.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Case_Content:
Woman, 63 years old, right-sided T4N2M1 colon cancer, two liver metastases in segments II and IVa (3 and 4 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. Liver MRI: middle hepatic vein preserved. CEA 95 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Technically resectable metastases, with priority given to controlling the primary tumor.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Justification:  
  • Imaging shows two isolated metastases in segments II (3 cm) and IVa (4 cm) with the middle hepatic vein preserved, indicating that an anatomic resection with negative margins is technically feasible.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease is identified on thoraco‑abdominal CT.  
  • High‑risk oncologic features (T4 primary, N2 nodal disease, KRAS mutation, CEA 95 ng/mL) raise concern for aggressive biology and suggest the need for systemic therapy before definitive liver surgery.  
  • The future liver remnant (FLR) volume and functional reserve have not been reported; without this data the case cannot be deemed outright resectable, thus it remains “potentially resectable” pending further assessment.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Induction systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 4–6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI ± anti‑VEGF).  
   – Rationale: Down‑size disease, treat micrometastatic burden, and serve as a biological test of tumor responsiveness given the high‑risk features.  

B. Surgical control of the primary tumor (right hemicolectomy) after the initial chemotherapy cycles, provided there is no acute obstruction, perforation, or bleeding.  
   – Rationale: MDT priority is primary‑tumor control; resection prevents local complications and allows accurate pathologic staging.  

C. Restaging work‑up (contrast‑enhanced CT chest/abdomen, liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast, and volumetric CT for FLR calculation).  
   – Rationale: Confirm response of liver lesions, verify that no new extra‑hepatic sites have appeared, and quantify FLR to ensure safe hepatic resection.  

D. Definitive hepatic resection (segmental resection of segments II and IVa, or left lateral sectionectomy plus segment IVa) aiming for R0 margins, provided FLR ≥ 20–30 % and adequate inflow/outflow.  
   – Rationale: Curative intent removal of all hepatic disease once systemic disease is controlled and liver reserve is confirmed.  

E. Adjuvant systemic therapy (completion of a total of 6–8 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy, adjusting regimen based on response and tolerability).  
   – Rationale: Improves disease‑free survival in high‑risk, KRAS‑mutated patients.  

If FLR is insufficient after step C, consider portal vein embolization or a two‑stage hepatectomy before proceeding to definitive liver surgery.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with two liver metastases located in segments II and IVa (3 and 4 cm), without evidence of extrahepatic disease. MRI confirms preservation of the middle hepatic vein and no major vascular invasion. Both lesions are technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections (in case of effective tumor shrinkage with neoadjuvant therapy) or left hepatectomy with preservation of the middle hepatic vein. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number and favorable anatomical location of metastases, this pattern is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Priority: control of the primary tumor
• The elevated CEA level (95 ng/mL) and right-sided T4N2 colon cancer represents locally advanced disease and is the immediate oncologic priority.
• Given the high CEA level (95 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Assess potential extension of primary tumor to adjacent organ (abdominal wall, ureter, small bowel, duodenum)
• 3 options
-	Perform an oncologic right hemicolectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis, first to control the primary tumor and prevent local complications.
-	Perform an derivation ileostomy first to control the primary tumor and prevent local complications during chemotherapy.
-	Initiate peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).

• Initiate peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• This period allows treatment of micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Liver surgery after restaging
• After 2–3 months of chemotherapy, perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan restaging.
• If tumor response is observed on primary cancer : proceed to oncologic right hemicolectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis
• If tumor response is observed on liver metastases, proceed to parenchymal-sparing resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segment II wedge/segmentectomy.
– Segment IVa wedge/segmentectomy.
• If stability or progression is observed, proceed to anatomic left hepatectomy preserving the middle hepatic vein guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis

Case_Content:
Woman, 70 years old, history of hypertension, discovery of left colon cancer and a single 2.7 cm liver metastasis in segment IVb at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 40 ng/mL. BRAF wild-type, MSS.
MDT Discussion: Isolated metastasis, anatomically favorable for a single resection.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Resectable (upfront resectable)  
- Rationale:  
  • Single liver metastasis, 2.7 cm, located in segment IVb – size < 3 cm and solitary lesions are within standard technical criteria for R0 resection.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease identified on thoraco‑abdominal CT (pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal, bone, brain assumed absent).  
  • No reported vascular or biliary invasion; therefore a limited anatomical resection (segmentectomy or wedge) is technically feasible while preserving ≥2 contiguous liver segments.  
  • Patient’s only reported comorbidity is hypertension; no evidence of liver dysfunction, suggesting adequate functional reserve.  
  • Molecular profile (BRAF‑wt, MSS) is favorable for long‑term outcomes.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Complete pre‑operative work‑up  
   – Obtain liver‑specific MRI (or contrast‑enhanced MRI) to confirm lesion characteristics, assess proximity to major vessels/ducts, and calculate future liver remnant (FLR) volume.  
   – Perform colonoscopy with biopsy if not already done, and stage the primary tumor (T/N status, grade).  
   – Assess performance status (ECOG/ASA), baseline liver function tests, and cardiopulmonary fitness.  

B. Determine sequencing of primary and liver surgery  
   – If the primary left‑colon tumor is asymptomatic (no obstruction, perforation, or bleeding) and the patient is fit, a simultaneous resection (left‑sided colectomy + segment IVb resection) is reasonable, given the limited hepatic operation and low operative risk.  
   – If the primary tumor is symptomatic, obstructed, or the patient’s operative risk is borderline, adopt a staged approach: first resect the primary colon cancer, allow recovery, then proceed to hepatic resection within 6–8 weeks.  

C. Peri‑operative systemic therapy  
   – Given synchronous disease and a CEA of 40 ng/mL (moderately elevated), discuss peri‑operative (neoadjuvant) chemotherapy (e.g., 3–4 cycles of FOLFOX ± biologic) to assess tumor biology (“test of time”) and potentially eradicate micrometastatic disease.  
   – If pre‑operative imaging confirms clear resectability and FLR is adequate, neoadjuvant therapy can be omitted, proceeding directly to surgery; otherwise, administer the short course and re‑image before hepatic resection.  

D. Post‑operative management  
   – Pathology review of resection margins (aim R0).  
   – Consider adjuvant chemotherapy (completion of 6‑8 cycles total) based on final pathology (node status, grade, vascular invasion).  
   – Schedule surveillance: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of liver and chest every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

   – Evaluate the primary colon lesion: colonoscopy, CT‑colonography if needed, and determine whether it is symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding, perforation).  

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy  
   – Initiate an oxaliplatin‑based doublet (e.g., FOLFOX) combined with bevacizumab (KRAS‑mutated disease) for 3–6 cycles.  
   – Rationale: high‑risk primary (T4 N2), elevated CEA, and to test tumor biology; also to potentially down‑size liver lesions and increase the chance of an R0 resection.  

C. Re‑assessment after chemotherapy  
   – Repeat liver MRI (or triphasic CT) and repeat FLR calculation.  
   – If disease is stable or responding and FLR ≥ 30 % (≥ 40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is suspected), proceed to hepatic surgery.  
   – If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy (first stage: clearance of lesions in the future liver remnant, followed by PVE).  

D. Surgical sequence  
   – Liver‑first approach (preferred when the primary is asymptomatic): perform anatomical or non‑anatomical resections of segments IV, V and VIII aiming for R0 margins while preserving at least two contiguous segments with adequate inflow/outflow.  
   – After hepatic recovery (≈ 6–8 weeks), perform definitive resection of the left‑sided colon primary (segmental colectomy with adequate lymphadenectomy).  
   – Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (continuation of the pre‑operative regimen) for a total of 6 months, adjusted for postoperative recovery.

Case_Content:
Woman, 74 years old, right T3N0 colon cancer, two liver metastases in segments III and VI (2.2 and 3 cm)at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 88 ng/mL, BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Anatomically accessible metastases, indication for primary surgery.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Rationale:  
  • Two liver metastases, both ≤3 cm, located in segments III and VI – technically amenable to anatomic segmentectomy or non‑anatomic wedge resection.  
  • No radiologically evident extra‑hepatic disease on thoraco‑abdominal CT.  
  • Bilobar distribution (left‑lateral and right‑posterior) raises concern for adequate future liver remnant (FLR) but the limited tumor burden suggests FLR could be ≥30 % in most patients; however FLR volume has not been measured.  
  • Patient age (74 y) and lack of reported performance status/comorbidities preclude a definitive “resectable” label without further fitness assessment.  
  • High CEA (88 ng/mL) and synchronous presentation (timing not documented) indicate biologically aggressive disease, favoring a short course of neoadjuvant chemotherapy to test tumor biology before definitive surgery.  

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Diagnostic completion – Obtain a liver‑specific MRI with diffusion‑weighted imaging and volumetric analysis; calculate FLR ratio; assess vascular and biliary anatomy; consider PET‑CT to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
B. Systemic therapy (neoadjuvant) – Initiate 2–3 cycles of a doublet regimen (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) to (i) treat micrometastatic disease, (ii) observe tumor biology (“proof of time”), and (iii) potentially downsize lesions.  
C. Re‑assessment after chemotherapy – Repeat imaging (MRI) to confirm disease stability or response and verify FLR adequacy.  
   • If FLR ≥ 30 % (or FLR/BW ≥ 0.5 %) and no progression, proceed to curative‑intent surgery.  
   • Surgical sequencing:  
     – Liver‑first (reverse) approach – Perform segmental resections of segments III and VI (or combined limited hepatectomy) first, followed by right hemicolectomy 4–6 weeks later. This is preferred because the primary tumor is asymptomatic, the liver surgery is limited, and it avoids potential delay of hepatic resection while treating the colon later.  
     – Simultaneous resection may be considered if intra‑operative FLR assessment confirms safety and the patient’s cardiopulmonary reserve is excellent.  
D. Adjuvant therapy – Complete peri‑operative chemotherapy to a total of 6 months (including neoadjuvant cycles) unless contraindicated; tailor biologic agent based on KRAS/NRAS status once available.  
E. Surveillance – Post‑operative CEA monitoring every 3 months for 2 years, cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) at 6‑month intervals, and colonoscopic surveillance per standard guidelines.

Case_Content:
Man, 49 years old, T2N0 rectal tumor associated with a single 2.8 cm liver metastasis in segment V at the abdominal CT scan, CEA 35 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Single metastasis, resectable upfront, surgery considered after local treatment of the primary.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable  
- Rationale:  
  • Single liver lesion, 2.8 cm, located in segment V – peripheral, amenable to non‑anatomic wedge or segmentectomy.  
  • No reported vascular, biliary, or portal invasion; therefore an R0 resection is technically feasible.  
  • A minor hepatectomy of segment V would preserve >2 contiguous liver segments and is expected to leave an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) in a 49‑year‑old without known liver disease.  
  • Absence of documented extra‑hepatic disease on imaging, but thoracic CT and liver MRI have not been performed; thus oncologic confirmation of isolated disease is pending.  
  • Primary rectal tumor is T2N0, asymptomatic (symptom status not reported), and has not yet been resected; its management will influence sequencing.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Complete staging  
   – Obtain thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary metastases.  
   – Perform liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast to confirm solitary lesion, assess vascular contact, and detect occult hepatic disease.  
   – Calculate FLR volume (CT‑volumetry or MRI) to verify that ≥30 % (≥40 % if pre‑operative chemotherapy is used) will remain.  

B. Neoadjuvant treatment of the rectal primary  
   – Deliver total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT): short‑course radiotherapy (5 Gy × 5) followed by consolidation chemotherapy (e.g., 6 cycles FOLFOX or CAPOX).  
   – Rationale: down‑stage the T2 lesion, address potential microscopic nodal disease, and provide an early test of tumor biology; also creates a treatment window for liver management.  

C. Restaging after TNT  
   – Repeat pelvic MRI and liver MRI to assess response of both primary and hepatic lesion.  
   – If the liver metastasis remains resectable and no new extra‑hepatic sites appear, proceed to surgery.  

D. Surgical phase  
   – Option 1 (simultaneous): Low anterior resection (TME) combined with a non‑anatomic wedge resection of segment V (or segmentectomy) in the same operation, provided operative risk is acceptable and FLR is adequate.  
   – Option 2 (staged – liver‑first): If the liver resection is deemed technically easier than the rectal operation, perform segment V resection first, followed 4–6 weeks later by TME after completion of TNT.  
   – Choice between simultaneous vs. staged should be individualized based on patient fitness, anticipated operative time, and surgeon expertise.  

E. Adjuvant systemic therapy  
   – Post‑operative FOLFOX (or CAPOX) for 3–6 months, given KRAS‑mutated disease and elevated pre‑operative CEA, to treat micrometastatic disease and reduce recurrence risk.

Case_Content:
Man, 57 years old, right T4aN2M1 colon cancer, seven bilobar liver metastases, sizes 1 to 4 cm at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 520 ng/mL, KRAS mutated. Liver MRI: vascular contact with the right portal branch.
MDT Discussion: Metastases not resectable upfront, considered for conversion chemotherapy FOLFOX + bevacizumab.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
• Current classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
• Rationale:  
  – Seven bilobar metastases (1–4 cm) exceed the traditional “≤4 lesions” rule and involve both hepatic lobes, making a single‑stage curative hepatectomy technically challenging.  
  – MRI shows vascular contact with the right portal branch, suggesting possible need for vascular reconstruction or portal vein embolization to obtain an adequate future liver remnant (FLR).  
  – FLR volume is not provided, but with bilateral disease and right‑portal involvement it is likely <30 % of total liver volume, a common threshold for unresectability.  
  – No extra‑hepatic disease is identified, so the limitation is purely hepatic.  
  – KRAS‑mutated tumor limits the benefit of anti‑EGFR agents but does not preclude response to oxaliplatin‑based doublet plus bevacizumab, which can achieve sufficient tumor shrinkage in many patients.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Induction (conversion) systemic therapy  
   – Start FOLFOX + bevacizumab (standard doublet with anti‑VEGF) for 3–4 cycles; consider escalation to FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab if the patient is young, fit (ECOG 0‑1) and liver function is preserved.  
   – Goal: tumor down‑staging, assess biological aggressiveness, and improve FLR by inducing atrophy of the diseased right lobe.  

B. Mid‑treatment reassessment  
   – Perform contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (including hepatobiliary phase) and repeat thoraco‑abdominal CT after 3 cycles.  
   – Evaluate: (i) reduction in size/number of lesions, (ii) persistence of right‑portal contact, (iii) calculation of FLR (volumetry).  
   – If FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % in steatotic livers) and all lesions are amenable to R0 resection, proceed to surgical planning.  

C. Pre‑operative liver optimisation  
   – If FLR remains insufficient, perform right portal vein embolization (PVE) or consider associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) in a high‑volume centre.  
   – Re‑image 2–3 weeks after PVE to confirm hypertrophy.  

D. Surgical phase (liver‑first approach)  
   – Perform curative‑intent hepatectomy aiming for R0 resection: likely an extended right hepatectomy with segment‑preserving resections of any left‑lobe lesions, or a two‑stage hepatectomy if residual left‑lobe disease persists after the first stage.  
   – Preserve at least two contiguous segments with intact inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  

E. Management of the primary colon tumour  
   – If the primary is asymptomatic and technically resectable, consider simultaneous colectomy after liver resection (provided operative time and patient condition allow).  
   – If symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding) or if simultaneous surgery would be unsafe, schedule a staged colectomy 4–6 weeks after hepatic recovery.  

F. Adjuvant/continuation therapy  
   – Resume the same systemic regimen (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) for a total of 6 months post‑hepatectomy, adjusting based on postoperative recovery and residual disease.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with seven bilobar liver metastases (1–4 cm) associated with vascular contact with the right portal branch and no reported extrahepatic disease. The number of lesions, bilobar distribution, and portal contact make a complete R0 resection with adequate future liver remnant unlikely with an upfront surgical approach. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered unresectable upfront.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Given the high CEA level (520 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Conversion systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Initiate intensive conversion chemotherapy with FOLFIRINOX + bevacizumab.
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• The objective is tumor downsizing, separation from portal structures, and reduction in the number/volume of lesions to achieve secondary resectability.

C. Early and repeated radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2-3 months to evaluate response, particularly the relationship of lesions to the right portal branch and overall liver tumor burden.
• Monitor CEA dynamics as a marker of response.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Consider surgery if chemotherapy induces:
– Reduction in lesion size and number allowing parenchymal-sparing resections or staged hepatectomy or combined resection and ablation.
– Clearance from portal structures.
– Feasibility of achieving R0 resection with adequate future liver remnant.

E. Potential surgical strategies if response is favorable
• Two-stage hepatectomy or combined parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern and tumor location.
• Portal vein embolization may be required if major hepatectomy becomes necessary.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. If no adequate response
• Continue second-line systemic therapy and/or consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).

Case_Content:
Woman, 60 years old, T3N1M1 sigmoid tumor, four bilobar liver metastases (segments II, III, VI, VIII) with one in contact with the right hepatic vein at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 240 ng/mL. RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar involvement for conversion, imaging to be re-evaluated after 4 cycles of chemotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
The patient is potentially resectable (borderline). Current imaging shows four bilobar metastases, one abutting the right hepatic vein, but no data on lesion size, future liver remnant (FLR) volume, hepatic functional reserve, or the need for vascular reconstruction. According to contemporary criteria, resectability hinges on achieving an R0 resection while preserving ≥30 % FLR (≥40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is present) and maintaining adequate inflow/outflow. Because these parameters are not provided, the disease cannot be declared outright resectable; however, it is not categorically unresectable and may become resectable after down‑staging chemotherapy and reassessment.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  

A. Conversion systemic therapy – Start 4–6 cycles of a doublet (mFOLFOX6) combined with an anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab) given RAS wild‑type status (alternatively FOLFOXIRI if tolerable). Goal: tumor shrinkage, assessment of tumor biology, and possible conversion to resectability.  

B. Restaging and volumetric assessment – After cycle 4, obtain a liver‑specific MRI (gadoxetate‑enhanced) with 3‑D volumetry to (i) measure the maximum diameter of each lesion, (ii) evaluate the relationship of the right‑hepatic‑vein‑contacting lesion, and (iii) calculate FLR percentage. Also repeat CEA and assess hepatic functional reserve (ICG‑R15, bilirubin, AST/ALT).  

C. Surgical planning based on restaging  
   • If FLR ≥ 30 % (≥ 40 % in the setting of chemotherapy‑related steatosis/steatohepatitis) and all lesions can be cleared with negative margins, proceed to curative liver resection.  
   • Options:  
      – Parenchyma‑sparing, multi‑segmental resections of segments II, III, VI, VIII, possibly with right‑hepatic‑vein reconstruction if tumor still contacts the vein.  
      – Two‑stage hepatectomy (first stage: clear the less‑affected lobe, portal vein embolization of the future remnant, then second‑stage extended resection) if FLR is insufficient after first‑stage clearance.  
      – ALPPS or PVE alone as alternatives if rapid hypertrophy is needed and patient fitness allows.  
   • Primary tumor management – If the sigmoid primary is asymptomatic (no obstruction, perforation, or bleeding) and the patient’s performance status is good, a simultaneous sigmoid resection can be performed during the liver operation. If symptoms are present or the operative time would be prohibitive, stage the primary resection first, then proceed with hepatic surgery after recovery.  

D. Post‑operative systemic therapy – Resume the same chemotherapy regimen (or switch to FOLFIRI ± anti‑VEGF if progression occurred) for 6 months as adjuvant treatment, aiming to eradicate microscopic disease and reduce recurrence risk.

According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy, but not safely resectable upfront.

– Relationship of the segment VIII lesion to the right hepatic vein.

• Surgery can be considered if imaging shows:

E. Potential surgical strategies if response is favorable

• If necessary, a two-stage hepatectomy strategy depending on response pattern and FLR considerations.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. If insufficient response
• Continue systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.

Case_Content:
Man, 63 years old, left T4N2M1 colon cancer, multiple liver metastases (≥8 lesions), maximum size 4.5 cm, partial contact with the IVC at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 890 ng/mL. BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Extensive liver disease, potentially resectable after major response to FOLFOXIRI.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Rationale:  
  • Multiple liver metastases (≥8) and bilateral distribution are high‑volume disease, but current guidelines no longer use lesion count as an absolute exclusion; resection can be considered if an R0 margin and adequate future liver remnant (FLR) are achievable.  
  • Largest lesion 4.5 cm is within size limits that can be addressed surgically.  
  • Partial contact with the inferior vena cava represents vascular involvement that may be resectable with vascular control or reconstruction, but it adds technical complexity.  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease (peritoneal and nodal disease assumed absent; pulmonary, bone, brain status unknown), therefore extra‑hepatic spread does not currently preclude hepatic surgery.  
  • BRAF wild‑type status and high CEA (890 ng/mL) suggest aggressive biology; however, response to intensive triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOXIRI) is anticipated to be a key biologic filter.  
  • FLR volume, liver function, and performance status are not provided; without these data a definitive “resectable” label cannot be applied. Hence the case fits the “potentially resectable after major response” scenario described by the MDT.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Continue/optimise systemic therapy  
   – Maintain FOLFOXIRI (± anti‑VEGF or anti‑EGFR based on RAS status) for additional cycles until maximal radiologic response is documented (RECIST ≥30 % reduction) and CEA trend shows significant decline.  
   – Rationale: systemic therapy serves both cytoreductive and biologic selection functions; a good response predicts favorable postoperative outcomes.  

B. Comprehensive restaging  
   – Perform contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific agent to delineate lesion number, segmental distribution, vascular relationships, and to calculate FLR (volumetry).  
   – Obtain thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) and bone scan/MRI to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
   – Repeat laboratory panel (LFTs, bilirubin, INR, albumin) and assess performance status (ECOG/ASA).  
   – Rationale: precise anatomic mapping and confirmation of disease confinement are prerequisites for surgical planning and for determining need of adjuncts (PVE, ALPPS).  

C. Decision point – conversion to surgery  
   – If imaging shows ≥30 % tumor shrinkage, FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 20 % in chemotherapy‑treated liver) and no new extra‑hepatic lesions, proceed to curative‑intent hepatic surgery.  
   – Surgical options:  
     • Two‑stage hepatectomy with portal vein embolization (PVE) after the first stage to hypertrophy the future remnant, given the high lesion count and bilobar disease.  
     • Associating Liver Partition and Portal vein Ligation for Staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) if rapid hypertrophy is required and patient fitness permits.  
     • Parenchymal‑sparing resections combined with IVC resection/reconstruction if vascular involvement is limited to the wall.  
   – Rationale: staged approaches maximize FLR while achieving R0 resection of all lesions; vascular reconstruction addresses IVC contact.  

D. Management of the primary colon tumor  
   – If the primary has not yet been resected and is asymptomatic, a liver‑first (reverse) strategy is preferred to avoid delaying potentially curative hepatic surgery.  
   – If obstructive or bleeding symptoms develop, perform urgent colectomy (or endoscopic stenting as bridge) before or concurrently with hepatic resection, depending on intra‑operative feasibility.  
   – Rationale: T4N2 disease warrants oncologic resection; sequencing should prioritize the organ with the greatest impact on survival while maintaining patient safety.  

E. Post‑operative adjuvant therapy and surveillance  
   – Resume systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) for 3–6 months post‑resection, tailored to pathologic response and molecular profile.  
   – Implement CEA monitoring every 3 months and cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with extensive bilobar liver metastases (≥8 lesions, up to 4.5 cm) with partial contact with the inferior vena cava and no reported extrahepatic disease. The tumor burden, bilobar distribution, and caval contact make a complete R0 resection with adequate future liver remnant not feasible with an upfront surgical approach. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered unresectable upfront, with a possibility of secondary resectability only after major tumor response.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI to define exact segmental distribution of all lesions with detailed vascular and biliary relationships. 
• Given the high CEA level (890 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Intensive conversion systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Initiate FOLFOXIRI combined with anti-EGFR therapy given RAS wild-type status as discussed in MDT.
• BRAF wild-type and MSS status do not modify the surgical indication.
• The objective is significant tumor downsizing, reduction in number/volume of lesions, and clearance from the IVC to enable potential surgical planning.

C. Close radiologic monitoring
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2-3 months to assess response, particularly:
– Relationship of lesions to the IVC.
– Global reduction of liver tumor burden.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as an indicator of treatment response.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
– Marked reduction in lesion size and number.
– Separation from the IVC.
– Feasibility of R0 resection with acceptable future liver remnant, potentially requiring staged hepatectomy with or without portal vein embolization.

E. Potential surgical strategies if response is favorable
• Two-stage hepatectomy or extensive parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern.

Response:

- Based on the limited information, the hepatic disease is potentially resectable (borderline) rather than clearly resectable or unresectable.  
- Rationale:  
  • Five bilobar metastases (segments II, III, IVa, VI, VII) each ≤ 4.1 cm, which is within size limits that can be addressed with parenchymal‑sparing or staged resections.  
  • No reported vascular or biliary invasion, but this data is missing; absence of such involvement would favor resectability.  
  • KRAS mutation and very high CEA (370 ng/mL) indicate aggressive biology, supporting the need for systemic down‑staging before surgery.  
  • Lack of documented extra‑hepatic disease; if truly absent, hepatic resection remains feasible.  
  • Critical technical factors (future liver remnant volume, portal/hepatic vein involvement, hepatic arterial anatomy) are not provided; therefore a definitive “resectable” label cannot be applied at this stage.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging  
   - Obtain contrast‑enhanced CT of chest, abdomen, pelvis and a liver‑specific MRI with diffusion‑weighted sequences.  
   - Evaluate for extra‑hepatic metastases (lung, peritoneum, nodes, bone, brain) and delineate vascular/biliary relationships of each lesion.  
   - Perform volumetric CT or MRI to calculate future liver remnant (FLR) and assess liver function (ICG clearance, bilirubin, AST/ALT).  

B. Systemic conversion chemotherapy  
   - Initiate an intensive doublet or triplet regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab) because KRAS is mutated (anti‑EGFR agents are contraindicated).  
   - Plan for 2–3 months (≈ 4–6 cycles) with radiologic assessment after every 2 cycles (RECIST 1.1).

   - If imaging shows ≥ 30 % reduction in total tumor volume and FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 25 % in a normal liver), proceed to curative‑intent liver surgery.  
   - Preferred approach: parenchymal‑sparing, anatomic or non‑anatomic resections of the five lesions, preserving at least two contiguous segments.  
   - If FLR is insufficient after response, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy (TSH) with interval chemotherapy.  

D. Management of the primary rectal tumor  
   - After hepatic disease is controlled (or concurrently if liver‑first strategy is chosen), treat the rectal primary with total mesorectal excision (TME).  
   - If the primary remains locally advanced, give neoadjuvant long‑course chemoradiotherapy (CRT) or total‑neoadjuvant therapy (TNT) before TME, following response assessment.  
   - Post‑operative (or post‑hepatectomy) adjuvant systemic therapy to complete a total of 6 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy.

Man, 62 years old, operated 4 years ago for right colon adenocarcinoma (T3N1M0), no initial recurrence. Surveillance: CEA 180 ng/mL. At the thoraco-abdominal CT scan: two liver lesions segments V and VIII, 2.8 and 3.2 cm. Liver MRI confirms no other foci. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.

Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Resectable (technically and oncologically)  
- Rationale:  
  • Only two metachronous liver metastases, each ≤ 3.5 cm, located in segments V and VIII – amenable to limited segmental resection or right‑hepatectomy with clear margins.  
  • No radiologic evidence of vascular or biliary invasion (information not provided but presumed absent).  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease on thoraco‑abdominal CT.  
  • Patient described as “good general condition,” suggesting adequate performance status and liver reserve.  
  • KRAS mutation and elevated CEA are adverse biological factors but do not preclude curative surgery when disease is limited.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (6 cycles of FOLFOX ± bevacizumab)  
   – KRAS‑mutated tumors do not benefit from EGFR antibodies; bevacizumab is appropriate.  
   – Provides a “biological test” of disease stability and treats micrometastatic disease.  

B. Restaging after neoadjuvant therapy (contrast‑enhanced liver MRI and CT)  
   – Confirm that lesions remain resectable, assess for new vascular contact, and calculate future liver remnant (FLR).  

C. Surgical resection (segmental resection of segments V and VIII, or right hepatectomy if FLR permits)  
   – Aim for R0 margins (>1 cm when feasible).  
   – Intra‑operative ultrasound to verify lesion boundaries and vascular anatomy.  
   – Ensure FLR ≥ 30 % of total liver volume (≥ 40 % if liver quality is compromised).  

D. Post‑operative (adjuvant) systemic therapy (additional 6 cycles of FOLFOX ± bevacizumab)  
   – Reduces risk of recurrence, especially given high pre‑operative CEA and KRAS mutation.  

E. Surveillance  
   – CEA every 2–3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  
   – Contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the chest/abdomen every 6 months for 3 years, then annually.

   The patient’s CEA is markedly elevated (95 ng/mL) but this alone does not preclude resection; it underscores the need for complete disease clearance.

A. Restaging and functional assessment  
   - Obtain a contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) and repeat liver MRI to confirm stability of the two lesions, exclude new extra‑hepatic sites, and measure the future liver remnant (FLR) volume.  
   - Perform liver function tests and assess performance status (ECOG/ASA).

   - If imaging confirms disease stability and FLR ≥ 30 % (≥ 40 % in compromised livers), proceed directly to surgery.  
   - If FLR is borderline or there is uncertainty about tumor biology, give a short course (2–3 months) of peri‑operative chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR antibody given RAS‑wild type) to serve as a “biologic test” and potentially downsize the micronodule.

   - Perform a parenchyma‑sparing resection: wedge/segmentectomy of segment II and segment V (or radiofrequency ablation of the micronodule if intra‑operative ultrasound confirms suitability).  
   - Aim for R0 margins (≥ 1 mm) with preservation of at least two contiguous segments, intact inflow/outflow, and adequate biliary drainage.

   - Resume/adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (6 months total, e.g., FOLFOX) given the high pre‑operative CEA and prior systemic exposure.  
   - Consider adding anti‑EGFR therapy (cetuximab) in the adjuvant setting if tolerated, based on RAS‑wild type status.

• Perform parenchymal-sparing wedge/segmental resections of segments III and VI guided by intra-operative ultrasound.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins.
