Case_Content:
Man, 66 years old, right colectomy for T4N2M0 cancer 24 months ago. FDG-PET: four liver foci, 1.5-3.5 cm, no extra-hepatic. KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Multiple metachronous liver involvement, surgical feasibility to be discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Rationale:  
  • Four metastases, each ≤3.5 cm, metachronous and without documented extra‑hepatic disease – favorable oncologic criteria.  
  • KRAS mutation does not preclude resection but influences systemic‑therapy choice.  
  • Technical resectability cannot be confirmed because critical data are missing: hepatic segment distribution, relationship to major vessels/bile ducts, and future liver remnant (FLR) volume.  
  • Without FLR assessment and vascular involvement information, a definitive “resectable” label is premature; thus the case is deemed potentially resectable pending further work‑up.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging  
   – Obtain high‑resolution triphasic abdominal CT and liver‑specific MRI (gadolinium‑EOB) with volumetric analysis to define segmental disease, vascular/biliary proximity, and calculate FLR (target ≥30 % in a normal liver or ≥40 % after chemotherapy).  
   – Perform chest CT (or PET‑CT if not already done) to reconfirm absence of pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic metastases.  
   – Repeat laboratory panel: liver function tests, bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count, and serum CEA.  

B. Systemic conversion chemotherapy  
   – Initiate an oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX) or triplet (FOLFOXIRI) combined with bevacizumab (anti‑VEGF) because KRAS is mutated and anti‑EGFR agents are ineffective.  
   – Plan 2–3 months (≈4–6 cycles) of therapy, monitoring toxicity and tumor markers.  

C. Re‑assessment after chemotherapy  
   – Repeat imaging (CT/MRI with volumetry) to evaluate tumor response (size reduction, possible disappearance) and to reassess FLR.  
   – If FLR remains inadequate (<30 %/0.5 FLR‑body‑weight ratio) consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a staged approach.  

D. Surgical intervention  
   – Goal: R0 resection with negative margins (≥5 mm acceptable) while preserving at least two contiguous liver segments with adequate inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
   – If disease is unilateral or can be cleared with a parenchymal‑sparing resection, proceed with single‑stage hepatectomy.  
   – If bilobar disease requires removal of >4 segments and FLR is marginal, adopt a two‑stage hepatectomy (first stage: clearance of lesions in the future remnant plus PVE; second stage after hypertrophy) or, in selected high‑volume centers, ALPPS with careful patient selection.  
   – Use intra‑operative ultrasound to detect occult lesions and guide resection.  
   – Post‑operative: resume/adjuvant systemic therapy (same regimen if tolerated) for 4–6 months.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four metachronous liver metastases (1.5–3.5 cm) without evidence of extrahepatic disease. Although multiple, the limited number and size of lesions suggest that parenchymal-sparing resections could achieve R0 margins while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited metachronous liver metastases, this pattern is considered resectable, pending precise anatomical assessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise segmental distribution and vascular/biliary relationships of the lesions.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• CEA dosage

B. Consider short peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the multiplicity of lesions and KRAS mutation, a short course (2–3 months) of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) is advisable to treat micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

D. Surgical management after restaging
• If resectability is confirmed, perform parenchymal-sparing resections of the four lesions guided by intra-operative ultrasound.
• Depending on distribution and FLR, a single-stage or staged approach may be selected.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Case_Content:
Woman, 71 years old, left colon cancer operated 5 years ago. Liver MRI: liver lesion segment V, 2.8 cm. CEA 90 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Isolated metastasis, favorable context, good general condition.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
• Classification: Potentially resectable (resectable pending confirmation of technical and oncologic criteria).  
• Rationale:  
  – Metachronous solitary liver lesion, 2.8 cm, located in segment V – size <3 cm and peripheral location are favorable for a parenchymal‑sparing resection.  
  – No reported vascular, biliary, or capsular invasion; therefore preservation of inflow/outflow and biliary drainage is likely feasible.  
  – Assuming the remaining liver can provide at least two contiguous segments, the anatomic requirement for resection is met.  
  – RAS wild‑type and long disease‑free interval (5 years) suggest biologically favorable disease.  
  – However, critical data are missing (complete thoraco‑abdominal staging, liver function, future liver remnant volumetry, exact number of lesions, and vascular relationship). Until these are confirmed, the lesion cannot be declared unequivocally resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging  
   – Obtain contrast‑enhanced CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis (or PET‑CT) to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
   – Perform liver function tests, indocyanine‑green clearance (or alternative quantitative liver function assessment), and calculate future liver remnant (FLR) volume from the MRI.  
   – Rationale: Definitive assessment of extra‑hepatic spread and FLR is mandatory before committing to surgery.  

B. Multidisciplinary decision point (after step A)  
   – If imaging confirms solitary disease, no extra‑hepatic metastases, and FLR ≥ 30 % (or FLR/BW ≥ 0.5 % in an elderly patient), proceed to curative‑intent hepatic surgery.  
   – If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage approach; if extra‑hepatic disease is present but limited and resectable, discuss combined or staged resections.  

C. Surgical intervention (when criteria satisfied)  
   – Perform a laparoscopic or open segment V wedge/segmentectomy with negative (≥1 mm) margins, preserving at least two contiguous segments and ensuring adequate inflow/outflow.  
   – Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm absence of additional occult lesions.  
   – Rationale: Parenchymal‑sparing resection minimizes postoperative liver failure risk while achieving R0 resection of the solitary metastasis.  

D. Adjuvant systemic therapy  
   – Recommend 6 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody given RAS wild‑type) either pre‑operatively (if borderline FLR) or post‑operatively, based on multidisciplinary consensus.  
   – Rationale: Improves disease‑free survival and treats micrometastatic disease; anti‑EGFR agents are appropriate in RAS wild‑type patients.  

E. Surveillance  
   – CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months; cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) at 6‑month intervals for 2 years, then annually.  
   – Rationale: Early detection of recurrence enables timely salvage therapy.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single metachronous liver metastasis in segment V (2.8 cm), without evidence of extrahepatic disease. The lesion is technically amenable to a parenchymal-sparing resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for solitary, metachronous, anatomically favorable metastasis, this pattern is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Perform high-resolution contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships.

B. Surgical management upfront
• Given the long disease-free interval and isolated liver involvement, immediate surgical resection is appropriate without mandatory neoadjuvant chemotherapy.
• Perform a segment V wedge/segmentectomy or ablation guided by intra-operative ultrasound aiming.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

C. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Initiate adjuvant doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic treatment.

D. Surveillance
• Close postoperative follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Case_Content:
Man, 64 years old, history of rectal resection (T3N1) 2 years ago. Liver MRI: two liver metastases, segments II and VIII, 2.5 and 3 cm. Thoracic CT scan negative for metastases. KRAS mutated, CEA 240 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar metachronous recurrence, technically accessible.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
- Justification:  
  • Technical factors – two lesions, each ≤3 cm, located in segments II and VIII; both can be removed with non‑anatomic segmentectomy or limited wedge resection, preserving a sufficient future liver remnant (FLR) in most adults.  
  • Oncologic factors – metachronous presentation, no radiologically evident extra‑hepatic disease, but adverse biology (KRAS mutation, markedly elevated CEA = 240 ng/mL) raises concern for early systemic progression; current practice often uses neoadjuvant chemotherapy (“proof of time”) before definitive liver surgery in such cases.  
  • No reported vascular or biliary invasion, no major hepatic vein/portal pedicle involvement, and no need for major hepatectomy, supporting technical feasibility.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., 2–3 months of FOLFOX ± bevacizumab or an equivalent doublet regimen).  
   – Rationale: addresses high‑risk biology (KRAS‑mutated, CEA > 200), provides “proof of time,” and may down‑size lesions if any occult microscopic spread is present.  

B. Restaging after chemotherapy (contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast, repeat thoraco‑CT, and assessment of liver function).  
   – Rationale: confirms that lesions remain resectable, evaluates FLR volume, and excludes new extra‑hepatic disease.  

C. Surgical resection – if FLR ≥ 30 % and no new contraindications:  
   – Preferred approach: simultaneous limited resections (segment II and segment VIII wedge/segmentectomy) preserving ≥ 2 contiguous segments of functional liver.  
   – If FLR is borderline (<30 %): consider portal vein embolization to induce hypertrophy or a two‑stage hepatectomy (first stage resection of the smaller lesion, then hypertrophy induction, followed by second stage).  

D. Adjuvant systemic therapy (3–6 months post‑operative, same or intensified regimen).  
   – Rationale: eradicates residual micrometastatic disease and improves disease‑free survival, especially in KRAS‑mutated, high‑CEA patients.  

E. Surveillance – CEA every 3 months for 2 years, cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with two metachronous liver metastases located in segments II and VIII (2.5 and 3 cm), without evidence of pulmonary disease. Although bilobar, both lesions are technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections or ablation while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited bilobar metachronous metastases, this pattern is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Perform high-resolution contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships and to calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Given the high CEA level (240 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to confirm absence of additional occult lesions.

B. Consider short peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the elevated CEA level (240 ng/mL) and relatively early recurrence (2 years), a short course (2–3 months) of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) is advisable to treat micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

D. Surgical management after restaging
• If resectability is confirmed, perform parenchymal-sparing wedge/segmental resections or ablation of segments II and VIII guided by intra-operative ultrasound.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Case_Content:
Woman, 58 years old, left T4aN2M1 colon cancer with multiple bilobar metastases. After 6 cycles FOLFOX + bevacizumab: 60% volumetric reduction, CEA dropped from 880 to 180 ng/mL. Liver MRI: 5 remaining lesions, well-defined.
MDT Discussion: Major response to chemotherapy, surgical conversion considered.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (conversion candidate).  
- Justification:  
  • After 6 cycles of FOLFOX + bevacizumab there is a 60 % volumetric reduction of the liver disease and CEA falls from 880 ng/mL to 180 ng/mL, indicating a favorable biological response.  
  • Imaging now shows only five well‑defined lesions bilobar, suggesting that a parenchymal‑sparing or staged hepatectomy may be feasible.  
  • However, critical data required to confirm technical resectability are missing (future liver remnant volume, exact lesion size and segmental distribution, vascular or biliary involvement, and presence/absence of extra‑hepatic disease). Without these, a definitive “resectable” label cannot be assigned; the case remains in the potentially resectable category pending further work‑up.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging (3–4 weeks)  
   - Perform contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal‑pelvic CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out extra‑hepatic metastases (lung, peritoneum, distant nodes, bone, brain).  
   - Obtain a high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast for precise lesion mapping (size, segment, relationship to major vessels/bile ducts).  
   - Calculate future liver remnant (FLR) volume using CT‑ or MRI‑based volumetry; aim for FLR ≥ 30 % of total liver volume in a normal liver or ≥ 40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is suspected.  
   - Assess liver function (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count, ICG clearance if available) and overall performance status (ECOG 0‑1).  
   - Determine molecular profile of the primary tumor (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI) and histologic grade.  
   - Verify whether the primary colon tumor has been resected or requires surgery; assess for obstruction, perforation, or bleeding.  

B. Multidisciplinary decision on operative approach (once restaging confirms no extra‑hepatic disease and adequate FLR)  
   - If FLR is sufficient and lesions are amenable to parenchymal‑sparing resections, plan a single‑stage, liver‑first hepatectomy with simultaneous or staged colon resection (depending on primary tumor status).  
   - If FLR is borderline (< 30 % after planned resections), adopt a two‑stage hepatectomy:  
        • Stage 1 – resect lesions in the future liver remnant (e.g., left‑lateral section) and place portal vein embolization (PVE) of the diseased lobe to induce hypertrophy.  
        • Wait 2–4 weeks for FLR growth, re‑evaluate volumetry, then proceed to Stage 2 – major resection of the embolized lobe (right or extended right hepatectomy).  
   - Consider ALPPS only if PVE fails to achieve adequate hypertrophy and the patient has excellent performance status, given its higher morbidity.  

C. Timing of surgery relative to bevacizumab  
   - Schedule liver surgery 6–8 weeks after the last bevacizumab dose to minimize wound‑healing complications; if needed, give 1–2 cycles of FOLFOX without bevacizumab in the interim to maintain disease control.  

D. Post‑operative oncologic management  
   - Resume systemic therapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) for a total of 6 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy, adjusting the regimen based on postoperative pathology and molecular status.  
   - Monitor CEA and obtain surveillance imaging (CT or MRI) at 3 months, then every 6 months for the first 2 years.  
   - Discuss enrollment in a clinical trial (e.g., conversion‑therapy or adjuvant targeted‑therapy trial) if available.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
After 6 cycles of FOLFOX + bevacizumab, the patient shows a major radiologic and biologic response (≈60% volumetric reduction; CEA from 880 to 180 ng/mL). MRI now demonstrates five well-defined residual liver lesions without reported extrahepatic disease. In this context of marked downsizing and clearer lesion delineation, a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant appears potentially achievable. This pattern is therefore considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Immediate high-quality restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to reassess precise segmental distribution and vascular/biliary relationships after tumor shrinkage.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical conversion strategy
• If imaging confirms feasibility, proceed to parenchymal-sparing resections or ablation of all five lesions guided by intra-operative ultrasound.
• Depending on distribution and FLR, this may be performed as a single-stage or staged hepatectomy.
• The goal is complete clearance of residual disease while preserving maximal functional parenchyma.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

C. Management of the primary tumor
• Left colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.
• A staged approach with colectomy first is preferred.

D. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Resume systemic chemotherapy after recovery to complete a total of approximately 6 months of treatment (including preoperative cycles).

E. Surveillance
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months given the initially very high tumor burden.

Case_Content:
Man, 65 years old, sigmoid tumor with eight bilobar liver metastases. After 4 months FOLFIRI: radiological stability, CEA unchanged at 420 ng/mL. Thoracic CT scan negative for metastases.
MDT Discussion: Stable disease, not resectable, discussion on continuing systemic therapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
- Rationale:  
  • Eight bilobar metastases exceed the classic “≤4 lesions” rule but current guidelines no longer use lesion count alone; resectability depends on ability to achieve an R0 resection while preserving ≥20‑30 % functional future liver remnant (FLR) and adequate vascular/biliary inflow‑outflow.  
  • Radiological disease is stable after 4 months of FOLFIRI, indicating no progression but also no tumor shrinkage; conversion to resectability therefore requires further down‑staging.  
  • CEA remains markedly elevated (420 ng/mL > 200 ng/mL), a negative prognostic factor that argues against immediate surgery without better disease control.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease on thoracic CT, but peritoneal, bone or other sites have not been evaluated.  
  • Because FLR, lesion size, vascular contact, and liver functional reserve are unknown, a definitive “resectable” label cannot be given; however, with appropriate down‑staging and hypertrophy strategies the case could become resectable.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Complete staging work‑up  
   - Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to define lesion size, exact segmental distribution, vascular/biliary involvement, and calculate FLR volume.  
   - Obtain contrast‑enhanced CT of abdomen/pelvis (if not already done) and consider PET‑CT to rule out occult extra‑hepatic disease (peritoneum, bone).  
   - Re‑biopsy primary tumor (if not already) for molecular profiling (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI‑H/dMMR) and confirm histologic grade.  
   - Assess liver function (ICG clearance, bilirubin, albumin) and patient performance status/comorbidities.  

B. Optimize systemic therapy (conversion intent)  
   - Switch to a more intensive regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) or add a targeted agent based on molecular results (anti‑EGFR for RAS‑wildtype left‑sided disease, anti‑VEGF otherwise).  
   - Continue for 2–3 months, monitoring response with RECIST criteria and serial CEA.  

C. Re‑assessment for surgical conversion  
   - If imaging shows ≥20 % reduction in total tumor volume or disappearance of ≥2 lesions, recalculate FLR.  
   - If FLR remains <30 % of total liver volume, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy.  
   - Plan a parenchymal‑sparing, two‑stage hepatectomy (or single‑stage if FLR adequate) aiming for R0 resection of all liver lesions.  

D. Management of the primary colorectal tumor  
   - If the primary sigmoid lesion is still in situ and asymptomatic, it can be resected after hepatic clearance (liver‑first approach) or simultaneously if the hepatic operation is limited to ≤2 segments and the patient’s operative risk is low.  
   - If obstructive or bleeding symptoms develop, prioritize primary tumor resection (or endoscopic stenting) before hepatic surgery.  

E. If conversion fails  
   - Continue systemic therapy with best‑available regimen and consider locoregional liver treatments (radiofrequency ablation, hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy, or stereotactic body radiotherapy) for residual disease.  
   - Maintain regular multidisciplinary review every 2–3 months.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with eight bilobar liver metastases and, after 4 months of FOLFIRI, shows radiological stability with persistently elevated CEA (420 ng/mL). The number of lesions, bilobar distribution, and absence of meaningful tumor downsizing make a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant not feasible. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered unresectable in the current setting.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Continuation and adaptation of systemic therapy
• Given the absence of radiologic response and stable high CEA, modification of the systemic regimen should be considered according to MDT discussion.
• The objective remains to achieve tumor downsizing sufficient to allow potential secondary resectability.

B. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2 months to detect any delayed response or change in lesion distribution.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation can be considered only if a significant reduction in lesion size and number occurs, enabling parenchymal-sparing resections or multiples ablations or staged hepatectomy with adequate future liver remnant.

D. Alternative local strategies
• If systemic therapy achieves only partial control, consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).

Case_Content:
Woman, 49 years old, metastatic rectal cancer, ten initial liver lesions, CEA 1200 ng/mL. On FOLFOXIRI: disappearance of three foci, 40% reduction of others.Liver  MRI: several lesions became hypo-intense.
MDT Discussion: Partial response, evaluation of segmental resectability.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Rationale:  
  • Partial radiologic response after FOLFOXIRI (3 lesions disappeared, remaining 7 reduced ≈ 40 % and now hypo‑intense) indicates favorable tumor biology and possible downsizing.  
  • The absolute number of residual liver lesions (≈ 7) is still high; without data on size, segmental distribution, vascular or biliary involvement, and future liver remnant (FLR) volume, a definitive R0 resection cannot be confirmed.  
  • No information on extra‑hepatic disease; its presence would shift the case toward unresectable or require combined modality treatment.  
  • Therefore, the case meets criteria for “potentially resectable” pending further anatomic and functional assessment.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging  
   – Perform contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatobiliary phase, and a thoraco‑abdominal‑pelvic CT (or PET‑CT) to define: lesion size, exact hepatic segments involved, relationship to major vessels/bile ducts, and presence of extra‑hepatic metastases.  
   – Calculate FLR using volumetry; obtain liver function tests (ICG clearance, bilirubin, albumin, platelets) to assess regenerative capacity.  

B. Multidisciplinary re‑evaluation  
   – Present updated imaging, laboratory, and performance‑status data to the MDT (hepatic surgeon, colorectal surgeon, medical oncologist, radiologist, interventional radiologist).  
   – Decide whether a single‑stage hepatectomy, a two‑stage hepatectomy, or portal vein embolization (PVE)/ALPPS is required to achieve adequate FLR.  

C. Surgical sequencing  
   – If the primary rectal tumor is asymptomatic and no urgent local control is needed, adopt a liver‑first approach: proceed with hepatic resection (or staged approach) after confirming resectability and adequate FLR.  
   – If FLR is insufficient, perform PVE (or consider ALPPS) and re‑image after hypertrophy before definitive hepatectomy.  

D. Management of the primary tumor and systemic therapy  
   – After hepatic surgery, reassess the rectal primary: if still present, plan total mesorectal excision (TME) or sphincter‑preserving surgery based on response; if a complete clinical response is documented, consider a watch‑and‑wait strategy with close surveillance.  
   – Continue systemic therapy post‑operatively (maintenance FOLFOXIRI or switch to a regimen guided by molecular profile) and incorporate targeted agents if RAS/BRAF status warrants.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After FOLFOXIRI, three lesions have radiologically disappeared and the remaining lesions show ~40% reduction, with several becoming hypo-intense on MRI. Despite this favorable response, the initial tumor burden and presumed bilobar distribution make immediate R0 resection uncertain without precise segmental mapping and volumetric assessment. This situation is therefore considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy, pending detailed re-evaluation.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging before any decision
• Perform high-quality liver MRI with diffusion sequences and compare meticulously with pre-treatment imaging.
• Identify the exact locations of the three “disappeared” metastases, as these sites may still harbor viable microscopic disease.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Assessment of true segmental resectability
• Determine whether all initial metastatic sites (not only visible residual lesions) can be encompassed within a surgical plan using parenchymal-sparing resections, staged hepatectomy, or combined resection/ablation.
• Intra-operative ultrasound will be essential to localize occult residual disease.

C. Surgical strategy if complete clearance is feasible
• If all initial sites can be addressed, proceed with an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing strategy, potentially in staged fashion depending on FLR.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. If complete clearance is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess after additional cycles.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Case_Content:
Man, 71 years old, metastatic right colon cancer (KRAS mutated). After 8 cycles FOLFOX: progression of two lesions segment VII and VIII (up to 5.2 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 950 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Progression on chemotherapy, no surgical window at this stage.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Unresectable (currently)  
- Rationale:  
  • Two liver metastases in segments VII‑VIII have grown to 5.2 cm despite 8 cycles of FOLFOX, indicating disease progression and aggressive tumor biology.  
  • KRAS‑mutated tumor limits efficacy of anti‑EGFR agents and is associated with poorer response rates.  
  • No liver‑specific volumetric data (future liver remnant) or detailed vascular anatomy are available; lesions in posterior segments often abut major hepatic veins, raising concern for vascular involvement.  
  • High CEA (950 ng/mL) supports active systemic disease.  
  • MDT already concluded “no surgical window at this stage,” reflecting consensus that an R0 resection cannot be achieved with the current disease burden.  

Step 2 – Recommended Strategy  
A. Confirm and address the primary colorectal tumor  
   - Determine whether the right‑colon primary has been resected; if not, plan a right hemicolectomy either after liver disease control or as a staged procedure, provided the patient’s performance status permits.  

B. Switch to second‑line systemic therapy  
   - Initiate FOLFIRI + bevacizumab (or consider FOLFOXIRI if the patient is fit) to attempt disease control, given progression on oxaliplatin‑based regimen and KRAS mutation.  

C. Re‑assessment after 2–3 months of second‑line therapy  
   - Perform high‑quality contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with diffusion and hepatobiliary phase, plus CT‑based volumetry to evaluate:  
     • Tumor response or further progression  
     • Vascular involvement (hepatic veins, portal branches)  
     • Future liver remnant (target ≥ 30 % in a chemotherapy‑treated liver).  
   - If lesions shrink to ≤ 5 cm and adequate FLR is confirmed, consider curative intent surgery (right posterior sectorectomy or extended right hepatectomy) possibly preceded by portal vein embolization if FLR is marginal.  

D. Locoregional or palliative options if disease remains unresectable  
   - For stable but unresectable lesions, discuss radio‑embolization (Y‑90) or stereotactic body radiotherapy to achieve local control.  
   - Percutaneous ablation (RFA/MWA) may be feasible for lesions ≤ 3 cm after down‑staging; otherwise, treat with systemic therapy alone.  
   - Enrolment in a clinical trial of novel agents or combination strategies should be considered.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient shows progression of liver disease under FOLFOX with enlargement of two lesions in segments VII and VIII (up to 5.2 cm) and markedly elevated CEA (950 ng/mL). This radiologic progression under systemic therapy indicates biologically aggressive disease and makes a complete R0 resection with adequate oncologic control not achievable at this stage. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable in the current setting.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Adaptation of systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Given progression on FOLFOX, a change of systemic regimen is required according to MDT decision (e.g., switch to FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• The objective is to regain disease control and potentially create a future surgical window.

B. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2 months to evaluate response to the new regimen.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation can be considered only if a significant radiologic response occurs, allowing parenchymal-sparing resection with adequate future liver remnant.

D. If disease remains progressive
• Continue systemic therapy and consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).
• Consider local palliative approaches if needed according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Woman, 62 years old, left colon adenocarcinoma with seven liver metastases. After 6 cycles FOLFOX + panitumumab: complete disappearance of four foci and reduction of others at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA normalized.
MDT Discussion: Radiological complete response in several segments, uncertainty regarding microscopic persistence.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable / borderline  
- Rationale:  
  • Systemic therapy (6 cycles FOLFOX + panitumumab) produced a radiologic complete response of four lesions and marked shrinkage of the remaining three, indicating good tumor biology and chemosensitivity.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease is identified on thoraco‑abdominal CT (pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal, bone, brain assumed absent).  
  • Current imaging lacks critical technical details (exact size, segmental distribution, vascular or biliary involvement of the residual lesions, and quantitative future liver remnant [FLR] assessment). Without confirmation that an R0 resection can be achieved while preserving ≥2 contiguous functional segments and an adequate FLR (≥20‑30 % in a normal liver, higher if chemotherapy‑induced injury), definitive resectability cannot be declared.  
  • Therefore, the case meets criteria for “potentially resectable” pending further anatomic evaluation.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Restaging with high‑resolution liver MRI (including diffusion‑weighted imaging) and volumetric FLR calculation  
   – Clarifies residual lesion size, exact hepatic segments, relationship to major vessels/bile ducts, and determines whether the FLR meets safety thresholds.  

B. Multidisciplinary reassessment (hepatic surgeon, colorectal surgeon, medical oncologist, radiologist) after MRI results  
   – If MRI confirms ≤3‑4 residual lesions amenable to parenchymal‑sparing resection with negative margins and adequate FLR, proceed to curative‑intent surgery.  

C. Surgical sequencing  
   – Liver‑first approach (resect liver metastases first) because the primary colon tumor has not been reported as resected and the patient is asymptomatic from the primary.  
   – Perform anatomic or non‑anatomic resections as dictated by lesion location, aiming for R0 margins; use intra‑operative ultrasound to detect any occult disease.  
   – If FLR is insufficient, consider pre‑operative portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy/ALPPS to augment remnant volume before definitive resection.  

D. Post‑operative management  
   – Resume systemic chemotherapy (FOLFOX) for up to 6 months post‑resection, omitting anti‑EGFR biologic (panitumumab) given prior exposure and potential cumulative toxicity.  
   – Continue surveillance with serial CEA and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3‑6 months.  

If MRI demonstrates unresectable disease (e.g., extensive bilobar involvement, vascular encasement, or inadequate FLR), continue systemic therapy with the same regimen or consider conversion strategies (e.g., addition of bevacizumab, intensification to FOLFOXIRI) and/or local ablative modalities (RFA/MWA) as bridge to future resection.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had seven liver metastases. After 6 cycles of FOLFOX + panitumumab, four lesions have radiologically disappeared and the remaining lesions have significantly decreased in size, with normalization of CEA. Despite this excellent response, the initial tumor burden and the phenomenon of “disappearing metastases” mean that viable microscopic disease may persist at the original sites. This situation is therefore considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy, but requires meticulous mapping of all initial metastatic locations before surgery.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion sequences and systematically compare with pre-treatment imaging.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, including those no longer visible.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy addressing initial disease map
• Plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided surgical approach that includes resection or ablation of all initial metastatic locations, not only residual visible lesions.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to identify occult residual disease.
• Depending on lesion distribution, this may require a staged approach.

C. Management of the primary tumor
• Left colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.
• A staged approach with colectomy first is preferred.

D. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Resume systemic therapy after surgery to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

E. If complete surgical clearance of all initial sites is not feasible
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess, or consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Case_Content:
Man, 55 years old, metastatic rectal cancer (RAS wild-type), ten initial liver lesions. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy,liver MRI: three residual lesions <2 cm, CEA decreased from 1100 to 80 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Major response, potentially curative situation to be surgically re-evaluated.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
The patient is potentially resectable.  
- Oncologic factors supporting potential resectability: RAS wild‑type, marked CEA decline (1100 → 80 ng/mL), major radiologic response with 7 of 10 lesions disappearing and only three residual lesions <2 cm.  
- Technical factors that are currently unknown but critical: exact hepatic segment distribution of the three lesions, relationship to major vessels or biliary structures, and calculated future liver remnant (FLR) volume.  
- No documented extra‑hepatic disease, but the absence of thoraco‑abdominal imaging is a gap; if truly absent, extra‑hepatic disease does not preclude resection.  
Because the necessary technical data are missing, the case cannot be declared outright resectable; however, the disease burden is low enough to consider conversion to resection after completing restaging.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging (2‑3 weeks)  
   • Perform contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatobiliary agent plus triphasic CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis (or PET‑CT if available) to exclude occult extra‑hepatic metastases.  
   • Conduct volumetric CT or MRI to calculate FLR; if FLR <30 % (or <40 % after chemotherapy‑induced injury) plan portal vein embolisation (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy.  
   • Re‑evaluate the rectal primary: determine whether it has been resected, its distance from the anal verge, and need for neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (CRT) based on MRI of the pelvis.  

B. Systemic therapy optimisation (if restaging confirms no progression)  
   • Complete a standard peri‑operative regimen (e.g., 6 cycles total of FOLFOX±biologic) to achieve maximal tumour control (“proof of time”).  
   • If the primary rectal tumour still requires CRT, deliver long‑course CRT now (8 weeks) and schedule surgery 6‑8 weeks after completion.  

C. Surgical intervention  
   • Liver surgery – aim for parenchyma‑sparing, anatomic or non‑anatomic resections of the three ≤2 cm lesions with ≥1 mm margins, preserving at least two contiguous segments and adequate inflow/outflow.  
   • Rectal primary – perform total mesorectal excision (TME) after liver resection (sequential) or concurrently if patient fitness permits and intra‑operative logistics allow.  
   • If FLR is insufficient, perform PVE first, re‑image after hypertrophy, then proceed with liver resection.  

D. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy  
   • Resume or complete postoperative systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 3‑6 months) tailored to response and tolerability.  
   • Consider adding targeted therapy (anti‑EGFR) given RAS wild‑type status, especially if postoperative CEA remains elevated.  

E. Surveillance  
   • CEA every 3 months, cross‑sectional liver imaging (MRI) and chest CT every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy, MRI shows only three residual lesions <2 cm and a major biologic response (CEA from 1100 to 80 ng/mL). Despite this marked response, the initial tumor burden and likely bilobar distribution require careful mapping of all original metastatic sites. This situation is considered resectable after conversion therapy, pending detailed segmental and volumetric reassessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion sequences and meticulous comparison with baseline imaging.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, including those no longer visible (“disappeared metastases”).
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy based on the initial disease map
• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach aiming to resect or ablate all original metastatic locations, not only the three visible lesions.
• Depending on distribution and FLR, this may require a staged hepatectomy.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

C. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Resume systemic therapy after surgery to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

E. If complete clearance of all initial sites is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess, or consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Case_Content:
Woman, 67 years old, T4N2M1 transverse colon cancer, multiple bilobar liver metastases, CEA 600 ng/mL. On FOLFOX: overall stability, two new lesions detected at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan.
MDT Discussion: Limited progression on treatment, question of changing protocol.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
• Classification: Potentially resectable / borderline.  
• Rationale:  
  – The patient has multiple bilobar liver metastases and a high CEA (600 ng/mL), indicating a high tumor burden.  
  – Systemic therapy (FOLFOX) has produced only “overall stability” with the appearance of two new lesions, i.e., limited radiologic progression, which by current oncologic criteria places the disease in the “borderline‑resectable” category (progression of existing disease or emergence of new lesions during optimal chemotherapy suggests the need for further down‑staging before surgery).  
  – No information is available on the number of lesions, maximal diameter, segmental distribution, vascular or biliary involvement, or future liver remnant (FLR) volume; these technical factors are essential to declare a lesion “resectable.” In their absence, a definitive “resectable” label cannot be applied.  
  – No extra‑hepatic disease has been identified on thoraco‑abdominal CT, which is favorable, but brain imaging is missing.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Molecular work‑up and optimization of systemic therapy  
   – Obtain tumor tissue (primary or metastatic) for RAS, BRAF, MSI/MMR status.  
   – If RAS wild‑type, consider adding an anti‑EGFR agent (cetuximab or panitumumab) to a more intensive regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI) to improve response rates; if RAS/BRAF mutated, consider anti‑VEGF (bevacizumab) continuation or switch to a different doublet.  
   – Goal: achieve maximal tumor shrinkage and assess biologic behavior (response vs. progression).  

B. Comprehensive radiologic reassessment  
   – Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to define lesion number, size, segmental involvement, vascular/biliary contact, and to calculate FLR volume.  
   – Repeat thoraco‑abdominal CT/PET‑CT to confirm absence of new extra‑hepatic sites; obtain brain MRI if clinically indicated.  
   – Evaluate liver function (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelets) and calculate standardized FLR (target ≥30 % for normal liver, ≥40 % if chemotherapy‑induced injury).  

C. Decision point – surgical sequencing  
   – If FLR adequate and all disease can be cleared with negative margins: proceed with a liver‑first (reverse) approach because the primary tumor has not yet been resected and there are no obstructive or bleeding symptoms reported. This avoids delaying treatment of hepatic disease while the primary can be addressed later.  
   – If FLR insufficient or lesions remain borderline: consider pre‑operative portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy (first stage: clear lesions in the future remnant, PVE; second stage: resect the diseased lobe).  
   – If the primary tumor becomes symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding, perforation) or if intra‑operative assessment shows it is easily resectable, a simultaneous colon and liver resection may be performed, provided the hepatic resection is limited (≤3 segments) and the patient’s physiologic reserve allows it.  

D. Post‑operative and adjuvant management  
   – Complete a full course of peri‑operative chemotherapy (e.g., 3–6 months post‑hepatectomy) tailored to molecular profile.  
   – Monitor CEA serially; aim for a ≥50 % decline as a surrogate of response.  
   – Enroll in regular surveillance (CT/MRI every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually).
Reference:

The patient has multiple bilobar liver metastases with the appearance of two new lesions while on FOLFOX, indicating disease progression under systemic therapy. The tumor burden, bilobar distribution, and ongoing progression make a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant not feasible at this stage. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable in the current setting.

A. Adaptation of systemic therapy (mandatory)
• The appearance of new lesions under FOLFOX indicates resistance to the current regimen.
• A change of systemic protocol is required according to MDT decision (e.g., switch to FOLFIRI ± targeted therapy depending on molecular profile).
• The objective is to regain disease control and potentially create a future surgical window.

B. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2 months to evaluate response to the new regimen.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation can be considered only if a significant radiologic response occurs, allowing parenchymal-sparing resection with adequate future liver remnant.

D. If disease remains progressive
• Continue systemic therapy and consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).
• Consider local palliative approaches if needed according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Man, 61 years old, left colon cancer, KRAS mutated. Ten initial liver metastases. After chemotherapy: three lesions not visualized, six stable, one progressing (segment VII, 5 cm) at the abdominal CT scan.
MDT Discussion: Heterogeneous response, feasibility of selective local treatment to be discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
• Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
• Rationale:  
  – After systemic therapy the patient has 7 radiologically evident liver lesions (6 stable, 1 progressing, largest 5 cm in segment VII).  
  – The number and size of lesions are within the range that can be addressed surgically if an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved and if vascular/biliary involvement is absent.  
  – No extra‑hepatic disease has been documented, but thoracic imaging has not been performed, so occult pulmonary metastases cannot be excluded.  
  – KRAS mutation does not preclude resection, although it predicts a lower response rate to anti‑EGFR agents.  
  – Because critical data required for a definitive technical assessment (FLR volume, vascular contact, liver function, performance status, comorbidities, and status of the primary colorectal tumor) are missing, the case cannot be declared outright resectable; it remains potentially resectable pending further work‑up.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  

A. Comprehensive restaging  
   – Perform a contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic disease.  
   – Obtain a liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast (Gd‑EOB) to delineate lesion number, size, vascular/biliary relationships, and to calculate FLR.  
   – Repeat serum CEA (and CA 19‑9) to assess tumor marker trend.  
   – Review performance status (ECOG), comorbidities, liver function tests, and volumetric analysis.  

B. Management of the primary colorectal tumor  
   – If the primary lesion has not yet been resected and is symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding, perforation) → urgent surgical resection (segmental colectomy) before or simultaneous with liver surgery, depending on patient fitness.  
   – If asymptomatic and resected already → no further colorectal surgery needed.  

C. Systemic therapy continuation / modification  
   – Continue the current oxaliplatin‑based regimen (e.g., mFOLFOX + bevacizumab) because KRAS‑mutated disease benefits from anti‑VEGF therapy.  
   – Re‑evaluate after 2–3 additional cycles; if the progressing lesion in segment VII shows further growth, consider switching to second‑line therapy (e.g., FOLFIRI + bevacizumab) to achieve disease control before local treatment.  

D. Local treatment of liver disease  
   – If restaging confirms adequate FLR and no vascular invasion, plan a curative‑intent hepatic resection: segmentectomy of segment VII plus parenchymal‑sparing resections of the remaining stable lesions (aim for R0 margins).  
   – If FLR would be insufficient or vascular involvement precludes safe resection, employ adjunctive locoregional therapies: percutaneous radiofrequency ablation or stereotactic body radiotherapy for the progressing lesion, combined with resection of the resectable lesions.  
   – Aim for complete eradication of all viable hepatic disease (R0 or R1 + ablation).  

E. Post‑operative/adjuvant phase  
   – Resume or complete a total of 6 months of peri‑operative systemic chemotherapy (same regimen if tolerated, otherwise appropriate second‑line).  
   – Serial imaging (CT or MRI) and CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had ten liver metastases. After chemotherapy, three lesions are no longer visualized, six remain stable, and one lesion in segment VII has progressed to 5 cm. This heterogeneous response, with persistent multifocal disease and one progressing focus, makes a complete R0 resection of all initial metastatic sites unlikely while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable at this stage, though selective local strategies may be considered.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Reassessment of systemic strategy
• The progressing segment VII lesion indicates partial resistance to current chemotherapy.
• Adaptation of systemic therapy should be discussed in MDT to regain global disease control.

B. Detailed restaging and mapping
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with comparison to baseline imaging to localize all initial sites, including the “disappeared” lesions.
• Assess the precise anatomy of the progressing segment VII lesion and overall tumor distribution.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

C. Consideration of selective local treatment
• If systemic control is regained, a combined strategy may be considered:
– Parenchymal-sparing resection of the progressing segment VII lesion.
– Possible ablation/resection of other accessible stable lesions.
• The objective would be cytoreduction rather than complete clearance unless all initial sites can be addressed.

D. If global control cannot be achieved
• Continue systemic therapy and consider local ablative techniques for symptomatic or dominant lesions.
• If systemic therapy achieves only partial control, consider alternative regimens (such as local ablative techniques or intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).

Case_Content:
Woman, 59 years old, metastatic rectal adenocarcinoma with initial bilobar involvement. After 6 cycles FOLFOXIRI: complete disappearance of lesions at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA normal.
MDT Discussion: Radiological complete response, need to assess risk of occult residual disease.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable / pending confirmation  
- Rationale:  
  • Thoraco‑abdominal CT after 6 cycles FOLFOXIRI shows complete radiologic disappearance of all liver lesions and normal CEA, suggesting no macroscopic disease.  
  • Current imaging does not demonstrate residual hepatic tumor, but absence of MRI, PET‑CT, and intra‑operative ultrasound leaves uncertainty about occult microscopic disease.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease is identified on CT; however, brain imaging is not reported.  
  • Resectability hinges on (a) confirmation that no viable liver metastasis remains, (b) assessment of the primary rectal tumor (resected or still present), and (c) adequate future liver remnant (FLR) if any hepatic resection were contemplated.  
  • Therefore, the case cannot be declared definitively resectable or unresectable; it remains potentially resectable pending further staging.

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging  
   - Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast and a PET‑CT to exclude occult hepatic or extra‑hepatic disease (including brain).  
   - Conduct pelvic MRI and flexible endoscopy of the rectum to evaluate response of the primary lesion; obtain biopsies if any residual mass is seen.  
   - Rationale: Imaging and endoscopic confirmation are required to rule out microscopic residual disease before committing to surgery.

B. Multidisciplinary reassessment  
   - Reconvene the MDT with the new imaging/biopsy results to decide on the need for surgical intervention on the primary tumor and/or liver.  
   - Rationale: Decision making must integrate tumor biology (molecular profile), patient fitness, and the presence/absence of residual disease.

C. Surgical plan (if residual disease is identified)  
   - Primary rectal tumor: If still present, plan total mesorectal excision (TME) or organ‑preserving approach (local excision or watch‑and‑wait) based on clinical complete response and MRI findings.  
   - Liver: If any viable lesion is detected, perform intra‑operative ultrasound; proceed with parenchymal‑sparing resection or ablative therapy (RFA/SBRT) ensuring ≥2 contiguous segments of functional liver remain (FLR ≥ 30 % in a normal liver).  
   - Rationale: Achieve R0 resection or complete ablation while preserving hepatic function.

D. Surveillance / adjuvant therapy  
   - If no residual disease is confirmed, adopt a strict surveillance protocol (CT/MRI every 3 months for the first 2 years, then 6 months).  
   - Consider adjuvant systemic therapy only if high‑risk molecular features (e.g., RAS/BRAF mutation, MSI‑high) are identified.  
   - Rationale: Early detection of recurrence is critical; adjuvant therapy may improve disease‑free survival in biologically aggressive tumors.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had bilobar liver metastases. After 6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI, CT shows complete radiological disappearance of all lesions and CEA has normalized. Despite this apparent complete response, the high risk of occult residual microscopic disease at the sites of the initial metastases makes the situation potentially resectable after conversion therapy, but not safely classifiable as disease-free without precise remapping of the original disease.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion-weighted sequences and compare meticulously with baseline imaging.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, even if no lesion is currently visible.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy based on the initial disease map
• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach targeting the original metastatic locations, not only visible lesions.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to detect occult residual disease.
• Depending on distribution, a staged approach may be required.

C. If surgical targeting of all initial sites is not feasible
• Continue systemic therapy and close imaging surveillance.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal strategy.

D. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• If surgery is performed, resume systemic therapy to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer with bulky metastases. After 8 cycles of chemotherapy: incomplete reduction, persistence of three lesions >5 cm. CEA 450 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Partial response insufficient, no criteria for immediate resectability.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline) – the patient has three hepatic lesions each >5 cm after 8 cycles of chemotherapy, indicating a high tumor burden that may require a major hepatectomy.  
- Justification:  
  • Number of lesions (3) and size (>5 cm) are within the range that can be converted to resectability with further down‑staging or liver‑volume augmentation.  
  • No documented vascular or biliary invasion, and no clear evidence of extra‑hepatic disease, so technical resection may be feasible.  
  • Persistent disease after optimal systemic therapy and a very high CEA (450 ng/mL) suggest aggressive biology, warranting careful reassessment.  
  • Critical data required to confirm true resectability (segmental distribution, FLR volume, vascular contact, extra‑hepatic sites) are missing; therefore the case cannot be declared outright resectable at this time.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Complete restaging – obtain contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or multiphase CT) with volumetric analysis, chest CT (or PET‑CT) and a full abdominal‑pelvic CT to define: hepatic segment involvement, vascular/biliary anatomy, future liver remnant (FLR) percentage, and presence of extra‑hepatic metastases.  
B. Molecular profiling of the primary tumor – test for RAS, BRAF, MSI‑H/dMMR and other actionable markers to guide choice of targeted agents in subsequent systemic therapy.  
C. Optimized systemic therapy – if molecular results indicate eligibility, switch to a second‑line regimen (e.g., FOLFIRI ± anti‑VEGF or anti‑EGFR depending on RAS/BRAF status) and continue for 2–3 cycles while monitoring response (RECIST, CEA trend). The goal is maximal tumor shrinkage and assessment of biological behavior.  
D. Conversion/augmentation plan –  
   • If imaging shows that a single‑stage resection would leave an FLR < 30 % (or < 20 % in a steatotic liver), plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy.  
   • If lesions are bilobar but amenable to a two‑stage hepatectomy, schedule first‑stage limited resection/ablation of lesions in the future remnant, followed by interval hypertrophy and second‑stage completion hepatectomy.  
E. Primary tumor management – assess for symptoms (obstruction, bleeding, perforation). If asymptomatic, adopt a “liver‑first” approach and defer colectomy until after hepatic clearance; if symptomatic, perform urgent resection or diverting stoma before or concurrently with liver surgery, depending on operative risk.  
F. Post‑operative care – after hepatic (and/or colonic) resection, resume adjuvant systemic therapy tailored to molecular profile, monitor CEA and imaging every 3–4 months, and consider peri‑operative strategies to protect liver parenchyma (e.g., avoidance of excessive intra‑operative blood loss, use of low‑central‑venous‑pressure anesthesia).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had bulky liver metastases. After 8 cycles of chemotherapy, there is only partial reduction with persistence of three large lesions >5 cm and persistently elevated CEA (450 ng/mL). The residual tumor burden and limited response make a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant not achievable at this stage. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable in the current setting.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Adaptation of systemic therapy (mandatory)
• The insufficient response to current chemotherapy requires modification of the systemic regimen or consider intra arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary cancer, according to MDT decision.
• The objective remains to achieve further tumor downsizing that may open a future surgical window.

B. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2 months to evaluate response to the new regimen.
• Given the high CEA level (450 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to confirm absence of additional occult lesions.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation can be considered only if a significant radiologic response occurs, reducing lesion size and allowing parenchymal-sparing resection with adequate future liver remnant.

D. If disease remains insufficiently responsive
• Continue systemic therapy and consider local palliative approaches if needed according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Man, 63 years old, operated two years earlier with a right hepatectomy for synchronous metastases from a left colon cancer. Surveillance: CEA 220 ng/mL. Liver MRI: two lesions segments II and III (2.1 and 3.4 cm). KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Contralateral liver recurrence, anatomically accessible, no extra-hepatic disease.
Response:

Woman, 70 years old, history of left R0 hepatectomy for liver metastases three years ago. CEA 180 ng/mL. Liver MRI: single lesion segment VIII (3.8 cm) in contact with the IVC. RAS wild-type.

Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable / borderline.  
- Rationale:  
  • Single metastasis, 3.8 cm, meets size criterion for resection.  
  • Prior left hepatectomy leaves only right‑liver parenchyma; removal of segment VIII must preserve at least two contiguous segments (e.g., V‑VI‑VII) with adequate inflow/outflow – technically feasible but limited.  
  • Tumor contacts the inferior vena cava, indicating possible vascular involvement; resection may require IVC resection or patch reconstruction, increasing technical complexity.  
  • No data on future liver remnant (FLR) volume, underlying liver quality, or extra‑hepatic disease; therefore definitive “resectable” cannot be confirmed without further assessment.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Complete staging  
   – Obtain contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal or bone metastases.  
   – Perform liver function tests, indocyanine‑green clearance (if available), and assess for steatosis or chemotherapy‑induced injury.  

B. Pre‑operative systemic therapy  
   – Initiate 2–3 months of modern doublet chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) given high CEA (180 ng/mL) and RAS‑wild‑type status, to (i) test tumor biology, (ii) potentially shrink the IVC‑adjacent margin, and (iii) treat occult micrometastatic disease.  

C. Volumetric and vascular planning  
   – Perform CT‑based volumetry to calculate FLR; target ≥30 % of total liver volume for a liver previously exposed to chemotherapy, or ≥20 % if liver parenchyma is pristine.  
   – If FLR is insufficient, plan portal vein embolization (PVE) of the right portal branches to hypertrophy segments V‑VI‑VII before definitive surgery.  
   – Review hepatic arterial and portal anatomy; map IVC relationship with 3‑D reconstruction.  

D. Surgical intervention (contingent on steps A‑C)  
   – If imaging confirms absence of extra‑hepatic disease, FLR is adequate (or has been augmented by PVE), and tumor response is favorable, proceed to curative‑intent resection: an anatomic segment VIII resection (segmentectomy) with en‑bloc IVC margin control; reconstruct IVC if required (patch or primary repair).  
   – Use intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion boundaries and exclude additional occult metastases.  
   – Aim for R0 margin; a sub‑centimetre margin is acceptable in the modern era.  

E. Post‑operative management  
   – Resume/adapt systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6‑month total peri‑operative regimen) as adjuvant therapy.  
   – Monitor CEA serially; schedule surveillance imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years.  

If any step reveals unresectability (e.g., extra‑hepatic disease, FLR <20 % despite PVE, inability to achieve safe IVC resection), shift to non‑surgical options: stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) or percutaneous ablation of the hepatic lesion combined with systemic therapy.

The patient is potentially resectable (borderline).

A. Comprehensive restaging  
   - Obtain contrast‑enhanced triphasic CT of the abdomen/pelvis (or repeat high‑quality MRI) with volumetric analysis to calculate FLR.

   - Add PET‑CT if there is any doubt about occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
   - Obtain molecular profile of the primary tumor (RAS, BRAF, MSI) and confirm histology of the colorectal primary (grade, lymph‑node status).

      potentially induce modest shrinkage of the segment V lesion, facilitating a parenchymal‑sparing resection.

Woman, 55 years old, history of left hepatectomy for synchronous metastases. Surveillance: CEA 560 ng/mL. Liver MRI: multiple lesions in right and left lobes (up to 4.5 cm). RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Diffuse liver recurrence, potentially non-curative.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Justification:  
  • Bilobar recurrence with multiple lesions up to 4.5 cm after a previous left hepatectomy implies a limited future liver remnant (FLR) and a high tumor burden.  
  • No imaging data are provided on vascular or biliary invasion, FLR volume, or extra‑hepatic disease; therefore technical unresectability cannot be confirmed, but the current situation is unlikely to allow a safe one‑stage curative resection.  
  • RAS wild‑type status and the absence of documented extra‑hepatic metastases keep the patient in a category where conversion (down‑staging) strategies may render resection feasible.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Restaging and full work‑up  
   – Obtain thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal, bone or brain metastases.  
   – Perform liver volumetry (CT or MRI) to calculate FLR percentage.  
   – Assess liver function (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelets), performance status (ECOG/ASA), and comorbidities.  
   – Review pathology of the primary tumor (location, grade, margins) and any prior systemic therapy.  

B. Systemic conversion therapy  
   – Initiate intensive chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI) combined with an anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab) because the tumor is RAS wild‑type.  
   – Aim for maximal tumor shrinkage and control of microscopic disease; treat for 2–3 months with imaging reassessment.  

C. Re‑assessment and liver‑targeted hypertrophy  
   – Repeat liver MRI with volumetry after systemic therapy.  
   – If sufficient tumor response but FLR remains <30 % (or <0.5 % body‑weight ratio), consider portal vein embolization (PVE) of the diseased lobe or an ALPPS approach, depending on the extent of disease and institutional expertise.  

D. Surgical resection (curative intent)  
   – When FLR is adequate and disease is confined to the liver, perform a parenchymal‑sparing repeat hepatectomy (right or extended right resection) or a staged two‑stage/ALPPS procedure to achieve R0 margins while preserving at least two contiguous segments with adequate inflow/outflow.  
   – Intra‑operative ultrasound to detect occult lesions and ensure complete clearance.  

E. Post‑operative management  
   – Resume adjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., 6 months of FOLFOX or CAPEOX) based on pathological response and margin status.  
   – Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3–4 months for the first 2 years.

- Classification: Potentially resectable (requires further technical confirmation).

  • Single intra‑hepatic lesion, 3.1 cm, located in segment VIII – size and number meet standard technical criteria for resection.

  • Elevated CEA (200 ng/mL) suggests biologically aggressive disease but does not, by itself, preclude resection when the disease is isolated.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging  
   – Obtain contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) and repeat liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to confirm absence of extra‑hepatic metastases and to delineate the relationship of the tumor to the middle hepatic vein.  
   – Perform volumetric CT or MRI to calculate the future liver remnant (FLR) volume after a planned segment VIII resection.  
   – Assess liver function (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count) and underlying parenchymal disease (steatosis, fibrosis).

   – If FLR is adequate and no extra‑hepatic disease is found, initiate 2–3 cycles of modern combination chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFIRI) with targeted agent based on molecular profile (once known).  
   – Use response (radiologic and CEA trend) to gauge tumor biology; stable disease or response supports proceeding to surgery.  

C. Surgical intervention  
   – If post‑chemotherapy imaging shows stable or regressed tumor and FLR ≥30 % (or ≥40 % if liver quality is compromised), perform a parenchymal‑sparing resection: segment VIII wedge or segmentectomy with preservation of the middle hepatic vein when possible; if venous involvement is confirmed, plan for limited venous resection and primary repair or patch reconstruction.  
   – Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion margins and exclude occult disease.  
   – Aim for R0 resection with ≥1 mm margin; use intra‑operative frozen section if needed.  

D. Post‑operative management  
   – Resume/adapt systemic chemotherapy (adjuvant) within 4–6 weeks, tailored to molecular profile and prior regimen.  
   – Serial CEA monitoring and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–4 months for the first 2 years, then at increasing intervals.  
   – Consider local ablative therapy (RFA/MWA) for any small residual or recurrent lesions that are not surgically amenable.

  • RAS wild‑type status favors response to anti‑EGFR‑based conversion chemotherapy, supporting a strategy to improve oncologic biology before surgery.

A. Comprehensive restaging (imaging & functional assessment)  
   – Obtain contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out extra‑hepatic metastases.

   – Preferred: parenchymal‑sparing segmentectomy of segment III (or non‑anatomic wedge) with intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion clearance and achieve R0 margins.
