– Parenchymal-sparing wedge/limited resections for accessible lesions.
– Thermo-ablation (microwave/RFA) for deep or multiple small nodules to preserve parenchyma.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to guide both resection and ablation.
• The goal is R0 resection while strictly preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles if administered.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Case_Content:
Woman, 59 years old, left T4N2M1 colon cancer with three liver metastases (2-4 cm) and two bilateral pulmonary nodules at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated, CEA 620 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Synchronous hepato-pulmonary involvement, discussion of sequential strategy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
• The patient has three liver metastases (2–4 cm) in a left‑sided T4N2 colon cancer and two bilateral pulmonary nodules.  
• Liver disease meets technical criteria for potential resection (≤5 lesions, each ≤5 cm) provided an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved and there is no major vascular or biliary invasion.  
• The presence of synchronous bilateral lung metastases makes the disease biologically more advanced (M1b). Current consensus considers isolated resectable lung disease acceptable, but simultaneous liver‑lung‑primary resection is not routinely recommended without confirming pulmonary resectability and adequate pulmonary reserve.  
• Because the primary tumor has not yet been resected (status unknown) and the FLR, hepatic segment distribution, and pulmonary lesion characteristics are not defined, the case cannot be classified as outright resectable.  
Classification: Potentially resectable (ESMO category 1) – curative intent is possible after systemic therapy and further anatomic assessment.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Induction systemic therapy – start a 2–3 month regimen of a fluoropyrimidine‑oxaliplatin doublet (e.g., FOLFOX) combined with bevacizumab (anti‑VEGF, since KRAS is mutated). Rationale: tumor‑shrinkage of liver and lung lesions, assessment of disease biology, and reduction of CEA.  

B. Restaging work‑up – after induction therapy obtain:  
   – Multiphasic liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast to define segmental involvement, vascular contact, and calculate FLR volume.  
   – High‑resolution chest CT (or PET‑CT) to measure pulmonary nodule size, relationship to bronchi/vessels, and to assess mediastinal/hilar nodes.  
   – Pulmonary function tests to confirm operative fitness.  
   Rationale: determine whether liver and lung disease are now resectable and whether FLR ≥30 % (or ≥40 % in compromised liver) is achievable.  

C. Liver‑first (reverse) approach – if hepatic disease is resectable and FLR is adequate (or can be augmented with portal vein embolization), perform hepatic resection first.  
   – Choose a minor or major hepatectomy based on lesion distribution; consider portal vein embolization beforehand if FLR is borderline.  
   Rationale: the primary colon tumor is asymptomatic, and early control of liver disease prevents progression beyond resectability; also allows low central venous pressure without compromising a fresh bowel anastomosis.  

D. Sequential treatment of extra‑hepatic sites – after hepatic recovery (≈6–8 weeks):  
   – If pulmonary nodules are limited (≤4 cm total, ≤2 per lung) and pulmonary reserve is sufficient, proceed with staged thoracic metastasectomy (video‑assisted or open, per surgeon discretion).  
   – Finally, address the primary colon cancer (segmental colectomy) once liver and lung resections are completed and the patient has recovered, unless the primary becomes symptomatic during the interval, in which case it should be resected earlier.  
   Rationale: staged approach respects organ‑specific recovery times, minimizes cumulative operative stress, and follows the “liver‑first” paradigm for asymptomatic primaries with synchronous metastases.
Reference:

From a hepatobiliary perspective, the liver disease appears technically resectable. • Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Sequential surgical strategy after response
• If disease control or response is observed:
	1.	Address the primary colon tumor if symptomatic or locally advanced : left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon primary) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) should be coordinated according to response and patient condition (ideally after liver surgery).
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for colectomy.

	2.	Perform parenchymal-sparing liver resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound : 
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to guide both resection and ablation.
• The goal is R0 resection while strictly preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.

• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
	3.	Plan pulmonary metastasectomy or ablative treatment in a staged manner.

E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, right colon adenocarcinoma, four liver metastases (1.5-3.8 cm) and nodular peritoneal involvement at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 950 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Hepato-peritoneal disease, not curable upfront, discussion of induction chemotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Unresectable (currently)  
- Justification:  
  • Presence of radiologically evident peritoneal nodular disease (extra‑hepatic metastasis) – peritoneal carcinomatosis is considered a contraindication to curative‑intent hepatectomy unless it is limited and amenable to complete cytoreduction, which is not documented.  
  • Four liver metastases ranging 1.5–3.8 cm; while technically resectable in isolation, the combination with extra‑hepatic disease shifts the overall oncologic assessment to unresectable.  
  • Extremely elevated CEA (950 ng/mL) – a high tumor marker is associated with aggressive biology and poorer outcomes after surgery.  
  • No information on hepatic segment distribution, vascular or biliary involvement, or future liver remnant (FLR) – inability to confirm that a margin‑negative (R0) resection preserving ≥2 contiguous segments and an adequate FLR (>30 % in a healthy liver) is feasible.  
  • Primary colorectal tumor has not been resected; ongoing primary disease further precludes a definitive liver‑first curative approach.  

Step 2 – Recommended Strategy  
A. Comprehensive Restaging & Molecular Profiling  
   - Obtain high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast, and a whole‑body FDG‑PET/CT to delineate all intra‑ and extra‑hepatic disease.  
   - Perform colonoscopy (if not already done) with biopsy of the primary tumor to determine histologic grade, KRAS/NRAS/BRAF mutation status, and microsatellite instability (MSI).  

B. Systemic Induction Therapy  
   - Initiate intensive neoadjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) tailored to molecular results.  
   - Goal: tumor burden reduction, potential conversion of liver lesions to resectable status, and assessment of disease biology (response vs progression).  

C. Re‑evaluation After 2–3 months  
   - Repeat contrast‑enhanced CT/MRI and PET/CT.  
   - Calculate FLR using volumetric software; consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) if a major resection would be required and FLR is insufficient.  

D. Decision Nodes  
   1. If systemic therapy yields ≥30 % reduction of all liver lesions and peritoneal disease remains limited (PCI ≤ 10, resectable nodules) → proceed to multimodal curative intent:  
      - Cytoreductive surgery (CRS) + HIPEC for peritoneal disease, followed by parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy (or staged hepatectomy) to achieve R0 resection of liver metastases.  
   2. If disease remains extensive or progresses → continue systemic therapy (possible switch to second‑line regimen) and consider palliative measures; surgery is not indicated.  

E. Post‑operative / Adjuvant Management  
   - If curative surgery is achieved, resume postoperative chemotherapy (e.g., 6 cycles of FOLFOX) and consider targeted agents based on molecular profile.  
   - Enroll in surveillance program with serial CEA and imaging every 3–6 months.
Reference:
Step 1 - The patient presents with four liver metastases (1.5–3.8 cm) associated with nodular peritoneal involvement on CT. The presence of peritoneal carcinomatosis indicates systemic dissemination beyond the liver and precludes a curative hepatobiliary surgical approach at this stage. According to oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable from a hepatobiliary perspective in the current setting.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and peritoneal lesions.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Given the high CEA level (950 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Induction systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) according to MDT decision to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control according to patient tolerance.
• This allows treatment of potential micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology before surgery.
• The goal is to evaluate tumor biology and potential response at both hepatic and peritoneal sites.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgical strategy
• Surgical re-evaluation may be considered only in the rare situation of major response with near-complete control of peritoneal disease and limited residual liver lesions.
• If disease control or response is observed:
	1.	Perform parenchymal-sparing liver resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound : 
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to guide both resection and ablation.
• The goal is R0 resection while strictly preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
2. Address the primary colon tumor if symptomatic or locally advanced : start with laparoscopic assessment to evaluate PCI score and consider en-bloc right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with cytoreductive surgery (i.e. excision of all peritoneal nodules) with or without HIPEC according to response and patient condition.
• The sequence (primary first vs liver-first) depends on technical considerations and necessity of HIPEC.

E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

F. If disease remains disseminated
• Continue systemic second-line chemotherapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Woman, 54 years old, mid-rectal T3N1 tumor with five bilobar liver metastases and a right lung metastasis at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. RAS wild-type, CEA 330 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Limited hepato-pulmonary involvement, evaluation of a possible combined approach.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (neither clearly resectable nor unresectable with the data provided).  
- Rationale:  
  • Five bilobar liver metastases can be addressed with modern hepatic techniques (extended or staged hepatectomy, portal vein embolisation, ALPPS, or combined resection‑ablation).  
  • A solitary right‑lung metastasis is technically amenable to wedge resection or segmentectomy, and limited extra‑hepatic disease does not automatically preclude curative intent.  
  • RAS wild‑type status and the absence of reported vascular invasion suggest a favorable biological profile.  
  • Definitive technical resectability cannot be confirmed because lesion size, segmental distribution, vascular/biliary involvement, and future liver remnant (FLR) volume are unknown.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., 6 cycles of FOLFOX ± anti‑VEGF or anti‑EGFR based on RAS wild‑type).  
   - Purpose: assess tumor biology, achieve possible down‑staging of liver lesions, treat micrometastatic disease, and allow time for optimal liver remnant planning.  

B. Comprehensive restaging after chemotherapy:  
   - Multiphasic liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to define size, number, segmental location, vascular contact, and to calculate FLR.  
   - High‑resolution chest CT (or PET‑CT) to characterize the lung nodule (size, location, mediastinal nodes).  
   - Pulmonary function tests to confirm operative fitness for lung resection.  

C. Multidisciplinary surgical planning based on restaging results:  
   - If FLR ≥ 30 % (or >0.5 % body weight) and no major vascular invasion, proceed with curative‑intent liver surgery. Options:  
     • Single‑stage major hepatectomy (if feasible) or  
     • Two‑stage hepatectomy/portal vein embolisation or ALPPS for insufficient FLR.  
   - Perform pulmonary metastasectomy (wedge or segmentectomy) either simultaneously with liver resection (if operative risk acceptable) or sequentially (liver first, then lung 4–6 weeks later).  

D. Management of the primary rectal tumor after hepatic (and pulmonary) control:  
   - If the rectal lesion remains asymptomatic, deliver short‑course radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) followed by total mesorectal excision (TME) 6–8 weeks later.  
   - If symptomatic or threatening margins, consider long‑course chemoradiotherapy before TME.  
   - Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy to complete systemic treatment course.

The patient presents with five bilobar liver metastases and a single right lung metastasis in the setting of a mid-rectal T3N1 tumor, without other reported sites. From a hepatobiliary perspective, the liver disease may be amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections provided adequate future liver remnant is preserved. This situation is considered potentially resectable within a multimodal, sequential curative strategy.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver and pelvic MRI and chest CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and lung lesions.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Thoracic surgical assessment of the lung metastasis is required.
• Pelvic MRI to integrate rectal treatment planning.
• Given the high CEA level (330 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Initial systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Start systemic doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• The objective is to assess tumor biology and confirm disease control at hepatic and pulmonary sites.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver and pelvic MRI, and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
– Significant reduction in lesion size and number in both liver and lung.
– Feasibility of staged or parenchymal-sparing resections with adequate future liver remnant.

E. Potential surgical strategies for liver metastases if response is favorable
• Two-stage hepatectomy or combined parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern.
• Portal vein embolization / venous deprivation / ALPPS may be required if major hepatectomy becomes necessary.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. Management of the rectal primary
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy with chemotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles.
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

G. Management of the single lung metastase
• Plan pulmonary metastasectomy or ablative treatment in a staged manner.
• Preoperative evaluation of respiratory function

I. If insufficient response and if disease remains disseminated
• Continue second-line systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.
• Continue systemic third-line chemotherapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

J. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

Case_Content:
Man, 62 years old, left colon cancer with six liver metastases and lymph node involvement of the hepatic pedicle at the abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated, CEA 780 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Liver involvement associated with extra-hepatic lymph nodes, unfavorable prognosis.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable / borderline.  
- Rationale:  
  • Six hepatic metastases exceed the traditional “≤4” cutoff but modern series show that number alone does not preclude resection if an R0 margin and adequate liver remnant can be achieved.  
  • Presence of hepatic‑pedicle (extra‑hepatic) lymph node metastasis is a high‑risk feature and is often considered a relative contraindication; however, limited nodal disease in the hepatoduodenal‑retropancreatic area can be resected when R0 is feasible.  
  • No data on future liver remnant (FLR) volume, vascular involvement, or the exact hepatic segments affected, all of which are required to confirm technical resectability.  
  • KRAS mutation and markedly elevated CEA (780 ng/mL) suggest aggressive biology, reinforcing the need for disease control before surgery.  
  • Consequently, the case is not outright unresectable but cannot be declared resectable without further down‑staging and detailed anatomic assessment.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Systemic conversion therapy  
   - Initiate an oxaliplatin‑based regimen (e.g., mFOLFOX6) combined with bevacizumab (KRAS‑mutated disease precludes anti‑EGFR antibodies).  
   - Goal: tumor shrinkage, control of hepatic‑pedicle nodal disease, and assessment of tumor biology (response vs progression).  

B. Restaging after 2–3 months  
   - Perform high‑quality contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (including hepatobiliary phase) and repeat CT of chest/abdomen.  
   - Obtain FDG‑PET/CT to delineate extra‑hepatic nodal burden and exclude occult pulmonary, bone, or brain metastases.  
   - Calculate FLR using volumetric software; if FLR < 30 % (or < 0.5 % / kg), plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or consider a two‑stage hepatectomy.  

C. Surgical sequencing  
   - If disease is down‑staged to allow R0 resection of all liver lesions and hepatic‑pedicle nodes, proceed with a liver‑first approach (major hepatectomy ± en‑bloc nodal dissection).  
   - Simultaneous resection of the primary colon tumor is considered only if the primary has not yet been removed, the patient is asymptomatic, and operative risk is acceptable; otherwise, resect the colon after hepatic recovery (interval 6–8 weeks).  

D. Adjuvant management  
   - Post‑operative continuation of systemic chemotherapy for a total of 6 months (or longer per oncologic protocol).  
   - Consider enrollment in a clinical trial or use of targeted agents based on emerging molecular data (e.g., BRAF, MSI status) if indicated.  

If restaging shows disease progression or inadequate FLR despite PVE, maintain systemic therapy and pursue palliative measures; curative surgery would not be advisable in that scenario.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with six liver metastases associated with lymph node involvement of the hepatic pedicle. The presence of extrahepatic nodal disease at the hepatic hilum reflects systemic dissemination and markedly unfavorable tumor biology. Even if the liver lesions were technically resectable, the oncologic context precludes a curative hepatobiliary surgical approach at this stage. This situation is therefore considered potentially resectable from a hepatobiliary perspective.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and thoraco-abdominal CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of liver lesions and other para-aortic enlarged lymph nodes
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Given the high CEA level (780 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Systemic therapy as primary strategy (mandatory)
• Initiate or adapt systemic chemotherapy according to MDT decision (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab;
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR).
• The objective is global disease control and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Radiologic reassessment after treatment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI and abdominal CT after 2–3 months to reassess liver disease and nodal involvement.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of response.

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgery (highly exceptional)
• Surgical re-evaluation could be considered only in case of major response with major regression of nodal disease and significant downsizing of liver lesions.
• Any surgical strategy would remain highly selected and dependent on sustained disease control.

E. Surgical management of liver metastases (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform multiple wedge/segmental resections or ablation guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Perform en-bloc lymphadenectomy of the hepatic pedicles 
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. Management of the primary tumor
• If the sigmoid tumor has not yet been resected, a simultaneous sigmoid colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis can be considered, provided the patient’s condition allows combined surgery.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.

G. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

Case_Content:
Woman, 70 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer, multiple bilobar liver metastases and a single cerebellar metastasis at the total body CT scan. CEA 860 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Systemic disease with brain involvement, neurological priority indication.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Rationale:  
  • Multiple bilobar liver metastases are present, but the exact number, size, segmental distribution and vascular involvement are unknown; without this data the technical feasibility of an R0 hepatic resection cannot be confirmed.  
  • A solitary cerebellar metastasis constitutes extra‑hepatic disease. Current guidelines consider limited, controllable extra‑hepatic lesions (e.g., solitary brain metastasis amenable to stereotactic radiosurgery or resection) as a scenario in which hepatic resection may still be pursued after systemic therapy.  
  • The primary tumor is T4N2, indicating high‑risk biology; lack of molecular profiling (RAS/BRAF, MSI) further limits prognostic assessment.  
  • No information on future liver remnant (FLR) volume, liver function, or patient performance status is available; these are essential to declare a lesion “resectable.”  
  • Consequently, the case falls into the “potentially resectable” category pending further staging, response to systemic therapy, and control of the brain lesion.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neuro‑oncologic control – Immediate stereotactic radiosurgery (or surgical resection if symptomatic) of the cerebellar metastasis to prevent neurologic deterioration and to achieve local control.  
B. Systemic induction therapy – Start a modern doublet chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) combined with a biologic agent (anti‑VEGF or anti‑EGFR according to molecular status once available). Aim for 4–6 cycles to assess tumor biology and to attempt down‑staging of hepatic disease.  
C. Restaging and functional assessment – After induction therapy, obtain:  
   • Contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or CT) with volumetry to define number, size, segmental involvement, vascular contact, and calculate FLR.  
   • Repeat brain MRI to confirm control of the cerebellar lesion.  
   • Full thoraco‑abdominal CT or PET‑CT to rule out additional extra‑hepatic sites.  
   • Assessment of performance status (ECOG), liver function (bilirubin, INR, platelets) and cardiopulmonary reserve.  
   Decision point: if imaging shows sufficient FLR (≥30 % in normal liver or ≥0.5 %/kg body weight) and all disease can be cleared with negative margins, proceed to hepatic surgery; otherwise continue systemic therapy or consider alternative local therapies.  
D. Surgical sequence (if resectable) –  
   1. Liver‑first approach: Perform a staged hepatectomy (e.g., right hepatectomy with portal vein embolization or ALPPS if FLR insufficient) to achieve R0 resection of all hepatic lesions.  
   2. Primary colon resection: After hepatic recovery (typically 4–6 weeks), resect the right colon primary (if not already removed) using an oncologic right hemicolectomy.  
   3. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy: Resume systemic chemotherapy ± targeted therapy for at least 3–6 months post‑operatively, tailored to response and molecular profile.  
   If at any point disease progresses or FLR remains inadequate, shift to a palliative intent (systemic therapy, liver‑directed ablative techniques, or best‑supportive care).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with multiple bilobar liver metastases associated with a cerebellar metastasis in the context of a right T4N2 colon cancer and markedly elevated CEA (860 ng/mL). The presence of brain metastasis indicates advanced systemic dissemination and excludes any curative hepatobiliary surgical strategy at this stage. From a hepatobiliary perspective, this situation is considered unresectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Neurological priority (mandatory)
• Immediate neurosurgical and/or radiotherapy assessment of the cerebellar metastasis is required as the first therapeutic step.
• The objective is neurological control and symptom prevention.

B. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and thoraco-abdominal CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of liver lesions
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Given the high CEA level (860 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

C. Systemic therapy after neurological stabilization
• Initiate or adapt systemic chemotherapy according to MDT decision once neurological status is stabilized.
• The objective is global disease control.

D. Radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI and full-body imaging after 2–3 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

E. Criteria for reconsidering liver-directed therapy (exceptional)
• Hepatobiliary surgical re-evaluation would be considered only in the rare situation of complete neurological control and major hepatic response, which remains highly unlikely.

Case_Content:
Man, 55 years old, rectosigmoid tumor, four liver metastases and pelvic peritoneal implants at the abdominal CT scan. BRAF wild-type, CEA 320 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Hepato-peritoneal involvement, possible multimodal strategy to be discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
- Rationale:  
  • Four hepatic metastases do not preclude resection if an adequate future liver remnant (FLR ≥ 30 % or ≥ 0.5 % body weight) can be preserved; the number alone is not a technical contraindication.  
  • Presence of pelvic peritoneal implants represents extra‑hepatic disease; current guidelines consider limited peritoneal disease amenable to cytoreductive surgery (CRS) as a relative, not absolute, contraindication to hepatic resection.  
  • BRAF wild‑type status and left‑sided (rectosigmoid) primary are favorable prognostic factors for conversion and resection.  
  • Very high CEA (320 ng/mL) suggests aggressive biology and warrants systemic therapy before definitive surgery.  
  • Critical missing data (FLR calculation, size and segmental distribution of liver lesions, vascular involvement, PCI of peritoneal disease, performance status) prevent a definitive “resectable” label at this stage.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy  
   – Initiate 4–6 cycles of doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI) with a biologic agent (anti‑VEGF or anti‑EGFR based on RAS status, which is currently unknown).  
   – Goal: achieve tumor shrinkage, assess disease biology (“proof of time”), and potentially lower the peritoneal cancer index.  

B. Comprehensive restaging  
   – Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to define lesion size, segmental involvement, vascular/biliary contact, and to calculate FLR volume.  
   – Obtain chest CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary metastases.

- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
- Rationale:  
  • Five hepatic metastases (multifocal, likely bilateral) exceed the classic “≤4” rule but modern criteria allow resection if an R0 can be achieved and sufficient future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved.

A. Systemic induction therapy (e.g., 2–3 months of FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab or FOLFOX + cetuximab given RAS‑wild type).  
   - Rationale: Treat micrometastatic disease, evaluate tumor biology, and attempt downsizing of hepatic lesions to facilitate parenchymal‑sparing resection; also provides a “test‑of‑time.”

   - Perform liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast, repeat thoraco‑abdominal CT, consider FDG‑PET‑CT, and calculate FLR using CT volumetry.

   - Perform parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy (e.g., non‑anatomic resections or limited segmental resections) aiming for R0 margins; consider intra‑operative ultrasound to locate all lesions.

   - Resect the transverse colon primary (segmental colectomy or extended right hemicolectomy) once the patient has recovered from liver surgery and systemic therapy is completed or paused.  
   - Perform pulmonary metastasectomy (bilateral wedge resections or segmentectomies) either in the same operative session as the colon resection (if pulmonary reserve permits) or as a separate thoracic procedure after colonic surgery.  
   - Rationale: Achieve complete macroscopic clearance of all disease sites; staging the operations reduces cumulative operative stress and allows optimal peri‑operative management.

   – Start a standard oxaliplatin‑based doublet (e.g., FOLFOX) combined with a VEGF‑targeted agent (bevacizumab) because KRAS mutation excludes anti‑EGFR antibodies.

   – If the iliac lesion is symptomatic or at risk of fracture, deliver palliative radiotherapy (e.g., 30 Gy in 10 fractions) or consider stereotactic body radiotherapy.

• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. Management of the rectal primary
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy with chemotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles.
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

G. Management of the single lung metastase
• Plan pulmonary metastasectomy or ablative treatment in a staged manner.
• Preoperative evaluation of respiratory function

I. If insufficient response and if disease remains disseminated
• Continue second-line systemic therapy or adapt regimen according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.

J. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis

• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

Case_Content:
Man, 65 years old, right T4N2 colon cancer, eight bilobar liver metastases and moderate peritoneal carcinomatosis at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 970 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Extensive hepato-peritoneal disease, goal of systemic control.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
• Classification: Unresectable (currently).  
• Rationale:  
  – Eight bilobar liver metastases imply a high intra‑hepatic tumor burden; without detailed segmental mapping and FLR calculation it is impossible to guarantee preservation of ≥2 contiguous segments with adequate inflow/outflow and a future liver remnant ≥30 % (or ≥0.5 % body weight).  
  – Moderate peritoneal carcinomatosis on CT represents extra‑hepatic disease; peritoneal involvement is a contraindication to curative‑intent hepatectomy unless the peritoneal disease is limited (low PCI) and can be addressed surgically (cytoreduction + HIPEC).  
  – Primary tumor is T4N2, indicating aggressive biology; CEA = 970 ng/mL is markedly elevated, suggesting high systemic tumor load.  
  – No information on vascular invasion, lesion size, or response to any systemic therapy; therefore a safe R0 resection of all disease cannot be assured.  
  – Consequently, according to contemporary oncologic and technical criteria, the disease is deemed unresectable at presentation, but potentially convertible after systemic therapy and further staging.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging  
   – Obtain thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary metastases.  
   – Perform liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to define lesion size, segmental distribution, vascular/biliary involvement, and calculate FLR.  
   – Assess peritoneal disease with diagnostic laparoscopy; record Peritoneal Cancer Index (PCI) and evaluate resectability of peritoneal implants.  
   – Complete molecular work‑up of the primary (KRAS/NRAS, BRAF, MSI‑H/dMMR, HER2) and determine tumor grade.  
   – Document performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidities.  

B. Systemic conversion therapy  
   – Initiate intensive first‑line chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) or FOLFOX/FOLFIRI with targeted agent selected according to molecular profile.  
   – Goal: tumor down‑staging, reduction of hepatic tumor volume, and assessment of disease biology (response vs. progression).  

C. Re‑assessment after 2–3 months  
   – Repeat liver MRI and CT chest; repeat diagnostic laparoscopy if peritoneal disease was borderline.  
   – Calculate post‑treatment FLR; if FLR < 30 % consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy (or ALPPS in highly selected cases).  
   – If peritoneal PCI ≤ 10–12 and disease appears resectable, plan combined cytoreductive surgery + HIPEC followed by staged liver resection (or simultaneous liver‑first approach if liver disease is dominant).  

D. Long‑term plan  
   – If conversion to resectable status is achieved, proceed with curative‑intent surgery (primary colon resection, liver resection with R0 margins, and peritoneal cytoreduction + HIPEC as indicated).  
   – If disease remains extensive or progresses, continue systemic therapy (maintenance biologic ± fluoropyrimidine) and consider enrollment in clinical trials or best‑supportive care.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with eight bilobar liver metastases associated with moderate peritoneal carcinomatosis in the context of a right T4N2 colon cancer and markedly elevated CEA (970 ng/mL). The presence of peritoneal dissemination combined with extensive bilobar hepatic disease excludes any curative hepatobiliary surgical approach at this stage. From a hepatobiliary perspective, this situation is considered unresectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and peritoneal lesions.
• Given the high CEA level (970 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Induction systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) according to MDT decision to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control according to patient tolerance.
• This allows treatment of potential micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology before surgery.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgical strategy
• Surgical re-evaluation may be considered only in the rare situation of major response with near-complete control of peritoneal disease and limited residual liver lesions.
• If disease control or response is observed:
	1.	Perform parenchymal-sparing liver resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound : 
• The goal is R0 resection while strictly preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.
2. Address the primary colon tumor if symptomatic or locally advanced : start with laparoscopic assessment to evaluate PCI score and consider en-bloc right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with cytoreductive surgery (i.e. excision of all peritoneal nodules) with or without HIPEC according to response and patient condition.
• The sequence (primary first vs liver-first) depends on technical considerations and necessity of HIPEC.

E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

F. If disease remains disseminated
• Continue systemic second-line chemotherapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Man, 59 years old, left T3N1M1 colon tumor, five bilobar liver metastases (1.5-3.5 cm). CEA 1150 ng/mL. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.Liver MRI: contact of segment VIII lesion with middle hepatic vein.
MDT Discussion: Technically resectable disease, high tumor marker suggests systemic risk.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline resectable)  
- Justification:  
  • Technical factors are acceptable – five lesions ≤3.5 cm, bilobar distribution, and MRI shows only contact (not invasion) with the middle hepatic vein, which can be managed with parenchymal‑sparing resection or limited vascular reconstruction.  
  • Biological factors are unfavorable: KRAS‑mutated tumor, extremely elevated CEA (1150 ng/mL), and T3N1 primary suggest aggressive disease and higher risk of early recurrence.  
  • Absence of documented FLR volume, performance status, and extra‑hepatic staging prevents a definitive “resectable” label; therefore the case fits the current concept of borderline (potentially) resectable disease that warrants neoadjuvant systemic therapy and reassessment.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive pre‑operative work‑up  
   – Obtain ECOG/ASA performance status, full comorbidity assessment, liver function tests, and calculate future liver remnant (CT volumetry or MRI).  
   – Perform thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude occult extra‑hepatic metastases.  
   – Measure CA 19‑9 and repeat CEA for baseline trend.  
   – Review arterial, portal and biliary anatomy (CT angiography) to plan resection and possible vascular control.  

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (conversion chemotherapy)  
   – Initiate a doublet regimen (FOLFOX) combined with bevacizumab (anti‑VEGF) because anti‑EGFR agents are ineffective in KRAS‑mutated disease.  
   – Duration: 2–3 months (≈ 6–8 cycles), with interim CEA monitoring.  
   – Goal: assess tumor biology (“proof of time”), achieve possible downsizing, and allow time for FLR hypertrophy if portal vein embolization is contemplated later.  

C. Restaging after neoadjuvant therapy  
   – Repeat liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast, CT chest, and volumetric assessment of FLR.  
   – Criteria to proceed to surgery:  
        • No new extra‑hepatic lesions;  
        • Disease stable or responding (RECIST ≤ 20 % reduction acceptable);  
        • FLR ≥ 30 % (≥ 40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury suspected).  
   – If FLR insufficient, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy; if vascular involvement progresses, evaluate need for hepatic vein reconstruction.  

D. Surgical phase  
   – Perform R0 resection of all hepatic lesions using a parenchymal‑sparing approach; resect or reconstruct the middle hepatic vein only if oncologically required and technically feasible.  
   – Decide timing of primary colon resection:  
        • If primary tumor still in situ and symptomatic, consider simultaneous colon resection;  
        • If asymptomatic, a staged colon resection after hepatic recovery may reduce operative stress.  
   – Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion clearance and assess margins.  

E. Post‑operative/adjuvant management  
   – Resume systemic therapy (same regimen or switch to FOLFIRI + bevacizumab) for a total of 6 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy.  
   – Serial CEA and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–4 months for the first 2 years.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with five bilobar liver metastases (1.5–3.5 cm), including a segment VIII lesion in contact with the middle hepatic vein, without reported extrahepatic disease. From a technical standpoint, complete clearance with parenchymal-sparing resections appears feasible while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is resectable. However, the very high CEA level (1150 ng/mL) suggests aggressive tumor biology and a high systemic risk.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to confirm the relationship of the 5 lesions to segment VIII vascular and biliary structures. Precise anatomical mapping is required to plan a safe parenchymal-sparing resection.
• Given the high CEA level (1150 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Preoperative systemic therapy
• The elevated CEA level (1150 ng/mL) and multiplicity of lesions suggest biologically active disease.
• Give 3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) to treat potential micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• This period treats micrometastatic disease and evaluates tumor biology.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and evaluate vascular/biliary relationships.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

D. Surgical management (staged strategy)
• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a first multiple atypical resection for the 5 lesions and/or segmentectomy 8 with en-bloc partial resection a the middle hepatic veine removing the 5 metastases, or a formal right hepatectomy if anatomically more appropriate, and if volume of the remnant liver is sufficient, aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin .
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
• After recovery, perform left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis 

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals given the elevated initial tumor marker (CEA 1150 ng/mL).

Case_Content:
Woman, 62 years old, right T4aN2M1 colon cancer, seven liver metastases (2-5 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 1600 ng/mL. BRAF V600E mutation, MSS.
MDT Discussion: Extensive liver disease, poor prognosis linked to molecular profile.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
- Rationale:  
  • Seven liver metastases ranging 2–5 cm do not automatically preclude resection; modern techniques allow multi‑lesion, bilobar disease to be addressed if an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease is reported, satisfying the oncologic requirement for curative intent.  
  • The primary tumor is T4aN2, indicating advanced local disease, and the tumor harbors a BRAF V600E mutation with a markedly elevated CEA (1600 ng/mL), both markers of aggressive biology that favor a neoadjuvant systemic approach before definitive surgery.  
  • Technical factors that could render the disease unresectable (vascular or biliary invasion, segmental distribution, FLR volume) are not provided; therefore, resectability cannot be confirmed at this stage, but conversion to resectable status is plausible with down‑staging and appropriate hepatic planning.  

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging  
   - Obtain high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast to delineate segmental involvement, vascular contact, and biliary anatomy.  
   - Perform PET‑CT (or brain MRI if neurologic symptoms) to exclude occult extra‑hepatic metastases.  
   - Assess performance status (ECOG), cardiopulmonary reserve, liver function tests, and calculate FLR (CT volumetry).  

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy  
   - Initiate an intensive regimen tailored to BRAF‑mutant mCRC (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab or the BEACON‑compatible combination of encorafenib + cetuximab ± binimetinib).  
   - Treat for 2–3 months, then re‑image to evaluate tumor response and biological behavior (“proof of time”).  

C. Re‑assessment for surgical conversion  
   - If imaging shows sufficient tumor shrinkage and FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 20 % in a non‑steatotic liver), plan hepatic resection.  
   - For inadequate FLR, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy.  
   - Aim for parenchymal‑sparing, margin‑negative (R0) resection; multi‑segmental or two‑stage hepatectomy may be required.  

D. Primary tumor management  
   - If the right‑colon primary is asymptomatic, a “liver‑first” strategy is preferred: complete hepatic clearance first, then resect the primary colon cancer.  
   - If obstructive or bleeding symptoms develop, schedule simultaneous or staged colectomy accordingly.  

E. Post‑operative systemic therapy  
   - Continue targeted systemic therapy (BRAF/EGFR inhibition) for at least 6 months post‑resection, adjusting based on postoperative pathology and tolerance.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with seven liver metastases (2–5 cm) in the setting of a right T4aN2 colon cancer and a BRAF V600E mutation with very high CEA (1600 ng/mL). Despite the disease being confined to the liver, the number of lesions, their size, and especially the unfavorable molecular profile indicate highly aggressive systemic tumor biology. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered unresectable upfront, as surgery would not provide meaningful oncologic benefit at this stage.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to confirm the relationship of the 7 lesions to vascular and biliary structures. Precise anatomical mapping is required to plan a safe parenchymal-sparing resection.
• Given the high CEA level (1600 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Systemic therapy as primary strategy (mandatory)
• The elevated CEA level (1600 ng/mL) and multiplicity of lesions suggest biologically active disease.
• Initiate intensive systemic therapy adapted to the BRAF V600E profile according to MDT decision : give 3-6 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) to treat potential micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.
• KRAS status is unknow but BRAF V600E profile is poor prognostic factor
• The objective is global disease control and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and evaluate vascular/biliary relationships.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation could be considered only in the rare situation of major radiologic and biologic response with marked reduction in number and size of lesions. 
• In this situation, first multiple atypical resections and ablation guided by ultrasound with the aim to obtain R0 margins.
• Any surgical consideration would remain highly selective.

E. If disease remains extensive
• Continue systemic therapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented management according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Man, 66 years old, T3N2 upper rectal cancer with four liver metastases at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 980 ng/mL, RAS wild-type, MSI-H.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar metastases with MSI-H profile opening discussion for first-line immunotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Rationale:  
  • Four bilobar liver metastases can be technically resectable if an adequate future liver remnant (FLR ≥ 30 % in a normal liver, ≥ 20 % after chemotherapy) can be preserved.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease is identified on thoraco‑abdominal CT, which satisfies the oncologic criterion for liver‑only disease.  
  • Critical anatomic details (size of each lesion, exact segments involved, proximity to major vessels or biliary structures) are not provided, preventing confirmation of R0 feasibility.  
  • The primary rectal tumor has not yet been resected; synchronous rectal cancer is a relative contraindication to simultaneous liver resection and may necessitate a staged approach.  
  • High CEA (980 ng/mL) suggests a high tumor burden, reinforcing the need for systemic therapy to achieve disease control (“proof of time”) before definitive surgery.  
  • MSI‑H status opens the option of first‑line immunotherapy, which may downsize liver lesions and improve resectability.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Induction systemic therapy – Start first‑line anti‑PD‑1 immunotherapy (e.g., pembrolizumab) given MSI‑H status, optionally combined with a short course of chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX) to address high tumor burden and to provide early disease control.  
   – Rationale: Immunotherapy yields high response rates in MSI‑H mCRC and may convert borderline lesions to resectable status; concurrent chemotherapy adds cytoreduction if needed.  

B. Neoadjuvant treatment of the rectal primary – Deliver total‑mesorectal‑excision‑compatible chemoradiotherapy (long‑course CRT) or total‑neoadjuvant therapy (TNT) after systemic induction, depending on response of the primary and patient tolerance.  
   – Rationale: T3N2 rectal cancer requires local control; TNT allows maximal downstaging and may permit organ‑preserving approaches if a clinical complete response is achieved.  

C. Restaging (8–12 weeks after induction) – Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast and pelvic MRI to:  
   – Measure residual lesion size, number, and segmental distribution.  
   – Assess vascular/biliary involvement.  
   – Calculate FLR volume (CT‑based volumetry).  
   – Evaluate response of the rectal tumor (mrTRG, DRE, endoscopy).  
   – Rationale: Precise anatomic data are essential to decide between upfront resection, portal‑vein embolization (PVE) and staged hepatectomy, or continuation of systemic therapy.  

D. Surgical phase – If restaging shows:  
   1. Adequate FLR (≥ 30 % or ≥ 20 % with prior chemotherapy) and no unresectable vascular invasion → proceed with a liver‑first staged approach:  
      – If FLR is marginal, perform right (or left) portal‑vein embolization to hypertrophy the future remnant, then complete hepatectomy 4–6 weeks later.  
      – Perform parenchymal‑sparing resections or combined anatomic/non‑anatomic resections to achieve R0 margins.  
   2. Persistent borderline FLR or unfavorable anatomy → consider local ablative therapies (thermal ablation or stereotactic body radiotherapy) for residual lesions after resection of the bulk disease.  
   – After hepatic surgery and recovery (≈ 6–8 weeks), proceed to definitive rectal resection (total mesorectal excision) if the tumor has not achieved a clinical complete response; otherwise, continue surveillance for organ preservation.  

E. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy – Resume immunotherapy (or switch to pembrolizumab maintenance) post‑operatively for at least 12 months, per current MSI‑H mCRC guidelines, and consider adjuvant chemotherapy if pathological high‑risk features are present.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four bilobar liver metastases in the setting of a T3N2 upper rectal cancer. Although technically the liver disease may be amenable to parenchymal-sparing resection, the very high CEA (980 ng/mL) and, most importantly, the MSI-H profile indicate a tumor biology that is highly responsive to immunotherapy. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable, but surgery is not the first step given the expected efficacy of systemic immunotherapy.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to confirm the relationship of the 4 lesions to vascular and biliary structures. Precise anatomical mapping is required to plan a safe parenchymal-sparing resection.
• Given the high CEA level (980 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. First-line systemic immunotherapy (mandatory)
• Initiate immunotherapy according to MDT decision as first-line treatment for MSI-H metastatic colorectal cancer.
• The objective is major tumor regression and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 2–3 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Surgical re-evaluation after response
• If a major radiologic response occurs, reassess segmental resectability.
• Plan biopsy of the primary rectal tumor and liver metastases to assess tumor response to immunotherapy
• Consider parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided liver resections only if residual lesions persist and complete clearance is feasible with adequate future liver remnant.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic immunotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals given the elevated initial tumor marker (CEA 1150 ng/mL).

Case_Content:
Woman, 70 years old, left T3N1M1 colon tumor, two liver metastases segments II and III (3.2 and 4.0 cm) at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 320 ng/mL, BRAF wild-type, HER2 positive.
MDT Discussion: Limited involvement but HER2 mutation may influence systemic therapeutic strategy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
• Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline‑resectable)  
• Rationale:  
  – Two liver metastases are limited to segments II and III, each ≤ 4 cm, which is technically amenable to a left‑lateral sectionectomy while preserving ≥ 30 % future liver remnant (FLR) in most adults.  
  – No imaging evidence of vascular or biliary invasion is provided, but the absence of reported contact suggests they are not encasing major vessels.  
  – Extra‑hepatic disease has not been documented; however, thoracic imaging has not been performed, so occult pulmonary metastases cannot be excluded.  
  – The primary colon tumor is staged T3N1M1, but its resection status and symptom burden are unknown; this influences the timing of hepatic surgery.  
  – Because key biological and technical data (FLR volume, vascular involvement, extra‑hepatic disease) are missing, definitive “resectable” status cannot be confirmed without further work‑up, thus the case is placed in the potentially resectable category pending completion of staging.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Complete staging work‑up  
   – Obtain a contrast‑enhanced thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary metastases.  
   – Perform liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast to delineate lesion morphology, vascular relationships, and to calculate FLR volume.  
   – Assess performance status (ECOG), comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve), and baseline liver function.  
   – Determine whether the primary colon tumor has been resected; if not, evaluate for obstruction, perforation, or bleeding.

   – Initiate HER2‑directed double‑treatment (e.g., trastuzumab + pertuzumab or trastuzumab + lapatinib) combined with a standard doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX).

        • Assess tumor biology (“proof of time”) and response of both hepatic and possible extra‑hepatic lesions,  
        • Potentially downsize lesions if vascular proximity is identified, and  
        • Treat micrometastatic disease early.  

C. Surgical plan after restaging  
   – If the primary colon lesion remains unresected and is asymptomatic, consider a simultaneous resection (colon resection + left‑lateral hepatectomy) provided operative risk is acceptable.

   – Aim for R0 margins (> 1 mm) on liver specimens; intra‑operative ultrasound should be used to confirm lesion clearance.  

D. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy  
   – Continue HER2‑targeted therapy post‑operatively for a total of 6–12 months, in line with emerging data for HER2‑amplified mCRC.  
   – Consider adjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., 3–6 months of FOLFOX) based on pathological response, nodal status, and multidisciplinary consensus.  
   – Enroll the patient in a clinical trial if available (e.g., HER2‑directed therapy in the peri‑operative setting).

Case_Content:
Man, 55 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer, nine bilobar metastases at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 2500 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.Liver  MRI: infiltration of the right portal pedicle.
MDT Discussion: Major liver involvement, vascular invasion compromising resectability.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
• Classification: Unresectable (currently)  
• Rationale:  
  – Nine bilobar liver metastases exceed the traditional numeric threshold for straightforward resection and imply a very high tumor burden.  
  – MRI demonstrates infiltration of the right portal pedicle, indicating major vascular involvement that would require complex reconstruction and jeopardizes the ability to preserve adequate inflow/outflow.  
  – No data on future liver remnant (FLR) volume; with extensive bilobar disease the FLR is likely insufficient (<20‑30 %).  
  – High CEA (2500 ng/mL) and KRAS‑mutated biology suggest aggressive disease and lower likelihood of durable R0 resection.  
  – The MDT explicitly stated “vascular invasion compromising resectability.”  
  – Absence of documented response to systemic therapy; at presentation the disease meets criteria for “initially unresectable” rather than “borderline resectable.”  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Systemic conversion chemotherapy (first line)  
   – Initiate an oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX) combined with bevacizumab (anti‑VEGF) because KRAS mutation precludes anti‑EGFR agents.  
   – Consider adding irinotecan (FOLFOXIRI) if the patient’s performance status and comorbidities allow, given the high tumor burden.  
   – Goal: achieve tumor shrinkage, especially reduction of portal pedicle involvement, and improve FLR by decreasing lesion volume.  

B. Re‑assessment after 2–3 months (or after 6 cycles)  
   – Repeat high‑resolution liver MRI with volumetric analysis to calculate FLR ratio.  
   – Evaluate radiologic response (RECIST) and biochemical response (CEA trend).  
   – If sufficient down‑staging occurs (e.g., reduction to ≤4 lesions, loss of vascular invasion, FLR ≥ 30 %), proceed to surgical planning.  

C. Portal vein embolization (PVE) or ALPPS (if needed)  
   – If FLR remains marginal after chemotherapy but the disease appears resectable, perform PVE to induce hypertrophy of the future remnant.  
   – In selected cases where rapid hypertrophy is required and the patient is fit, ALPPS may be considered, acknowledging its higher morbidity.  

D. Surgical phase (liver‑first approach)  
   – Perform an anatomic or parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy aiming for R0 resection, preserving at least two contiguous segments with adequate inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
   – If portal pedicle invasion persists, vascular reconstruction (e.g., portal vein resection and reconstruction) should be undertaken only in centers with expertise and after confirming oncologic benefit.  
   – Following hepatic resection and recovery, schedule definitive resection of the primary right‑colon tumor (segmental colectomy) as a second stage, unless the primary becomes symptomatic earlier.  

E. Adjuvant/maintenance systemic therapy  
   – Continue postoperative chemotherapy (same regimen or switch to FOLFIRI) for 6 months, tailored to response and toxicity.  
   – Consider enrollment in a clinical trial if available (e.g., novel targeted agents for KRAS‑mutated disease).  

F. If down‑staging fails  
   – Maintain systemic therapy with possible switch to second‑line regimen (FOLFIRI + bevacizumab).  
   – Evaluate locoregional options for liver disease (radiofrequency ablation, stereotactic body radiotherapy) for lesions not amenable to resection.  
   – Provide best supportive care and symptom‑directed interventions.

From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered unresectable at this stage.

A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships.
• Given the high CEA level (2500 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgery (exceptional)
• Surgical re-evaluation could be considered only if a major response occurs with regression of portal pedicle involvement and significant reduction in tumor burden.

Case_Content:
Woman, 61 years old, T3N1M1 rectal tumor, three liver metastases (segments IVa, VI, VIII). CEA 680 ng/mL. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type. Liver MRI: extension to the hepatic vein confluence.
MDT Discussion: Metastases near venous confluence, high surgical risk.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Justification:  
  • Three hepatic lesions are confined to segments IVa, VI and VIII, which can be addressed with an extended right hepatectomy or combined segmental resections.  
  • MRI demonstrates tumor contact/extension to the hepatic‑vein confluence, a known technical challenge that may require vascular reconstruction and reduces the likelihood of achieving an R0 margin without complex surgery.  
  • No data on future liver remnant (FLR) volume; without confirmation that an adequate FLR (>30 % in chemotherapy‑naïve patients, >40 % after systemic therapy) can be preserved, the case remains borderline.  
  • High surgical risk noted by the MDT further supports a “potentially resectable” designation, indicating the need for down‑staging and careful peri‑operative planning before definitive resection.  

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Systemic induction therapy – Initiate intensive neoadjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± anti‑VEGF antibody) for 2–3 months, with radiologic reassessment thereafter.  
   • Rationale: aims to achieve tumor shrinkage, assess tumor biology (“proof of time”), and improve the chance of R0 resection while also treating micrometastatic disease.  

B. Restaging and functional assessment – Repeat liver MRI (or contrast‑enhanced CT) and obtain a volumetric CT to calculate FLR. Perform CT‑based chest/abdomen/pelvis to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
   • Rationale: determines whether the liver lesions have become resectable, confirms adequacy of FLR, and rules out contraindicating extra‑hepatic metastases.  

C. Adjunctive liver‑directed measures (if needed) – If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS).  
   • Rationale: safely augment future liver volume to meet the functional threshold for major hepatectomy.  

D. Definitive hepatic surgery – Proceed with curative‑intent liver resection (extended right hepatectomy or combined segmental resections) with vascular reconstruction of the hepatic‑vein confluence if required, aiming for R0 margins ≥1 cm.  
   • Rationale: after successful down‑staging and FLR optimization, the liver‑first approach offers early control of the dominant metastatic burden and avoids progression while the rectal primary is being managed.  

E. Management of the rectal primary – After hepatic recovery (typically 4–6 weeks), deliver standard neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy for the T3 N1 rectal tumor, followed by total mesorectal excision (TME) with appropriate sphincter‑preserving or abdominoperineal technique.  
   • Rationale: rectal cancer requires chemoradiation for local control; sequencing after liver resection reduces the risk of delaying curative hepatic surgery in a patient with high‑risk vascular involvement.  

F. Adjuvant systemic therapy – Complete postoperative chemotherapy (e.g., 6 months total, incorporating agents used in induction) based on postoperative pathology and tolerance.  
   • Rationale: consolidates disease control and addresses any residual microscopic disease.

Case_Content:
Man, 64 years old, left colon adenocarcinoma with four bilobar liver metastases. CEA 900 ng/mL, RAS wild-type. Liver MRI: segment VII lesion invading the IVC over 1 cm.
MDT Discussion: Caval invasion requiring multidisciplinary surgical evaluation.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Justification:  
  • Four bilobar metastases meet criteria for borderline disease (multiple lesions, bilobar distribution).  
  • One lesion in segment VII shows >1 cm invasion of the inferior vena cava, representing major vascular involvement that makes an R0 resection technically demanding and requires complex reconstruction.  
  • No data on future liver remnant (FLR) volume, primary tumor status, or extra‑hepatic disease; these unknowns preclude a definitive “resectable” label.  
  • High CEA (900 ng/mL) and RAS wild‑type suggest aggressive biology, supporting the need for systemic therapy first to test disease control.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging  
   – Obtain thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) and high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast.  
   – Evaluate extra‑hepatic sites (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes, bone, brain).  
   – Perform volumetric CT to calculate FLR; assess hepatic arterial, portal venous, and biliary anatomy.  
   – Cardio‑pulmonary assessment (ECOG/ASA, cardiology clearance) given planned major hepatectomy and IVC reconstruction.  

B. Systemic induction therapy  
   – Initiate intensive neoadjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab) because of high tumor burden and CEA.  
   – Aim for ≥ 30 % radiologic response and to observe disease kinetics (test of biology).  
   – Re‑evaluate CEA trend after 2–3 cycles.  

C. Re‑assessment of resectability (after 2–3 months of therapy)  
   – Repeat liver MRI and FLR volumetry; if FLR < 30 % consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or ALPPS to hypertrophy.  
   – Determine if IVC invasion has regressed; if not, plan for en‑bloc IVC segmental resection with graft or patch reconstruction (vascular surgery input).  
   – Confirm that all hepatic lesions can be cleared with negative margins while preserving ≥ 2 contiguous liver segments.  

D. Surgical sequence (contingent on successful reassessment)  
   1. Primary‑first or liver‑first?  
      – If the primary colon tumor is still in situ and symptomatic, perform simultaneous colon resection and liver resection (if operative risk acceptable).  
      – If the primary is asymptomatic, a liver‑first approach is preferred to treat the most life‑threatening disease first and to allow postoperative chemotherapy before colon surgery.  
   2. Liver operation  
      – Extended right hepatectomy (or appropriate anatomic resection) with IVC segmental resection and reconstruction using PTFE or autologous graft.  
      – Use intra‑operative ultrasound to locate any occult lesions; consider adjunctive ablation for marginal disease.  
   3. Post‑operative management  
      – Early postoperative chemotherapy (e.g., continuation of the same regimen or switch to maintenance) for at least 3–6 months.  
      – Surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months for the first year.

Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four bilobar liver metastases, including a segment VII lesion invading the IVC over ~1 cm, without reported extrahepatic disease. While the number of lesions is limited, true caval invasion makes a standard parenchymal-sparing R0 resection unlikely without complex vascular resection/reconstruction and carries high operative risk. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable only in a highly selected setting, after tumor downsizing and multidisciplinary vascular assessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI to define exact segmental distribution of all lesions with detailed vascular and biliary relationships. 
• Given the high CEA level (900 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Intensive conversion systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Initiate FOLFOXIRI combined with anti-EGFR therapy given RAS wild-type status as discussed in MDT.

C. Close radiologic monitoring
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2-3 months to assess response, particularly:
– Relationship of lesions to the IVC.
– Global reduction of liver tumor burden.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as an indicator of treatment response.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
– Marked reduction in lesion size and number.
– Separation from the IVC.
– Feasibility of R0 resection with or without partial IVC resection with acceptable future liver remnant, potentially requiring staged hepatectomy with or without portal vein embolization.
• Multidisciplinary evaluation with vascular surgery is required to assess feasibility of partial IVC resection/reconstruction if needed.

C. Surgical management if feasibility is confirmed
• One or two-stage hepatectomy or extensive parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern.
• If regression of caval invasion occurs or reconstruction is deemed feasible, plan an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resection of all lesions.
• Anticipate possible IVC tangential resection or graft reconstruction.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

• After recovery, perform left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis

• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
