• Continue systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.

Case_Content:
Woman, 58 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer, five liver metastases including one 8.5 cm in segment IVb at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 870 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Large central metastasis with bilateral portal contact, complex technical discussion.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
• Classification: Potentially resectable / borderline.  
• Justification:  
  – Five hepatic lesions, including an 8.5 cm central metastasis in segment IVb, exceed the traditional “≤3 cm” and “≤4 lesions” thresholds but modern criteria allow resection if complete clearance and adequate FLR are achievable.  
  – Presence of bilateral portal vein contact indicates technical complexity and may compromise inflow/outflow, raising concern for a safe margin and for preserving vascular integrity.  
  – No extra‑hepatic disease is identified on thoraco‑abdominal CT, which favors a curative intent approach if hepatic clearance can be obtained.  
  – Absence of data on future liver remnant (FLR) volume, hepatic functional reserve, and response to systemic therapy prevents a definitive “resectable” label; therefore the case is best considered borderline pending down‑staging and volumetric assessment.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Systemic induction therapy – Administer 4–6 cycles of intensive doublet or triplet chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI) combined with an anti‑VEGF agent (bevacizumab) given KRAS mutation. Rationale: assess tumor biology, achieve tumor shrinkage, and potentially convert the large central lesion to a resectable size while providing early treatment of occult disease.  

B. Restaging and functional assessment – After induction, obtain high‑resolution liver MRI with diffusion‑weighted imaging and hepatic venous phase CT; perform volumetric analysis to calculate FLR, and assess portal/hepatic arterial anatomy (including any encasement). Evaluate liver function (ICG clearance, bilirubin, albumin, coagulation) and patient performance status (ECOG/ASA). Rationale: determine whether a single‑stage resection is feasible or whether hypertrophy strategies are required.  

C. Hypertrophy / staged approach (if needed) –  
   – If FLR < 30 % (or < 20 % in compromised liver), proceed with portal vein embolization (PVE) of the liver segments to be resected, or consider ALPPS/associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy.  
   – Re‑image 4–6 weeks later to confirm adequate hypertrophy. Rationale: increase safe residual liver volume to permit major hepatectomy.  

D. Definitive hepatic resection (liver‑first) –  
   – When adequate FLR and clear vascular inflow/outflow are confirmed, perform an anatomic or parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy targeting all five lesions with negative (R0) margins; intra‑operative ultrasound and possible adjunctive ablation for lesions difficult to resect.  
   – If the primary right‑colon tumor has not yet been removed and is asymptomatic, schedule a right hemicolectomy either simultaneously (if the hepatic resection is limited to ≤3 segments and the patient’s operative risk is acceptable) or as a second‑stage operation after hepatic recovery. Rationale: liver‑first strategy minimizes the risk of hepatic progression while allowing definitive treatment of the primary once the patient has recovered from major liver surgery.

Case_Content:
Man, 73 years old, transverse colon tumor, two liver metastases (4.2 and 4.8 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 70 ng/mL. BRAF wild-type, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Normal CEA despite high volume, question regarding biological sensitivity for follow-up.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline resectable)  
- Rationale:  
  • Two liver metastases, each ≤5 cm, which meets the size and number criteria for technical resectability.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease identified on thoraco‑abdominal CT.  
  • Favorable tumor biology (RAS‑wild, BRAF‑wild) and a CEA of 70 ng/mL (below the 200 ng/mL high‑risk threshold).  
  • Age 73 y does not preclude surgery, but performance status and comorbidities are unknown.  
  • Critical technical data are missing (exact hepatic segments involved, proximity to major vessels or bile ducts, future liver remnant (FLR) volume, liver function). Without these, a definitive “resectable” label cannot be given; therefore the case is best described as potentially resectable pending further assessment.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Complete restaging  
   – Obtain a high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to delineate lesion anatomy, vascular/biliary relationships, and to calculate FLR.  
   – Perform a PET‑CT (or high‑resolution chest CT if not already done) to exclude occult extra‑hepatic metastases.  
   – Review laboratory data (bilirubin, INR, platelets, albumin) and assess ECOG performance status and comorbidities.  

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (if technically borderline or to obtain “proof of time”)  
   – Initiate 2–3 months of doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI) combined with an anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab) given RAS‑wild status.  
   – Re‑image after 2 cycles to assess radiologic response and confirm that disease remains stable or regresses.  

C. Surgical plan (based on reassessment after step A/B)  
   1. If FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 20 % with normal liver) and no vascular invasion:  
      – Proceed to curative‑intent resection.  
      – Preferred sequence: resect the transverse colon primary (segmental colectomy with oncologic margins) first, followed by liver resection 2–3 weeks later (or simultaneous if operative risk acceptable).  
   2. If FLR insufficient or vascular involvement is present:  
      – Perform portal vein embolization (PVE) of the liver segments to be resected and re‑evaluate FLR after 4–6 weeks.  
      – Consider a two‑stage hepatectomy or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) only in highly selected, fit patients.  

D. Adjuvant therapy  
   – After R0 liver resection (and primary tumor resection), give 6 months of postoperative chemotherapy (same regimen as neoadjuvant) unless contraindicated.  
   – Enroll in surveillance program: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the liver every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

Case_Content:
Woman, 60 years old, left T4N1M1 colon cancer, six liver metastases (up to 5.6 cm) at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 1400 ng/mL. KRAS G12C mutation confirmed.
MDT Discussion: Specific molecular profile, may benefit from a later targeted strategy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
- Rationale:  
  • Six hepatic lesions, the largest 5.6 cm, exceed the classic “≤4 cm or ≤5 lesions” cut‑offs used for upfront resection, placing the disease in a borderline category.  
  • KRAS G12C mutation predicts limited benefit from anti‑EGFR antibodies and is associated with a more aggressive biology, supporting the need for down‑staging before surgery.  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease, but thoracic imaging and full liver MRI are missing; without confirmation of absence of pulmonary or other metastases the case cannot be declared clearly resectable.  
  • Future liver remnant (FLR) volume and vascular involvement are unknown; if FLR < 30 % or major vascular invasion is present the disease would be unresectable, otherwise conversion to resectability is feasible.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Complete staging  
   - Obtain thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary metastases.  
   - Perform liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to define segmental distribution, vascular/biliary involvement, and to calculate FLR.  
   - Assess performance status (ECOG), liver function tests, and comorbidities.  

B. Conversion systemic therapy  
   - Initiate oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX) combined with bevacizumab (KRAS‑mutated disease).  
   - Plan 3–4 months (≈6–8 cycles) with imaging reassessment after every 2–3 cycles.  
   - Monitor CEA trend; a falling CEA supports tumor response.  

C. Re‑assessment and surgical planning  
   - If imaging shows ≥30 % reduction in total tumor volume and FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % in steatotic liver), proceed to curative‑intent hepatectomy.  
   - Options based on lesion distribution:  
     • Single‑stage anatomical resection if all lesions can be cleared with adequate FLR.  
     • Two‑stage hepatectomy with portal vein embolization (PVE) or ALPPS if FLR is initially insufficient.  
   - Simultaneous resection of the primary colon tumor should be performed if the primary remains in situ and the patient is fit; otherwise, schedule colon resection first (primary‑first) or after liver surgery (liver‑first) according to symptomatology.  

D. Post‑operative systemic strategy  
   - Resume the same chemotherapy backbone (FOLFOX + bevacizumab) for 4–6 months as adjuvant therapy, or switch to FOLFIRI + bevacizumab if oxaliplatin toxicity limits continuation.  
   - Consider enrollment in a clinical trial or off‑label use of a KRAS‑G12C inhibitor (e.g., sotorasib) in the maintenance phase, given the specific molecular profile.

Case_Content:
Man, 57 years old, low T3N2M1 rectal cancer, four peripheral liver metastases (2-3.5 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 90 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, MSS, positive circulating tumor cells.
MDT Discussion: Presence of circulating cells despite low volume, prognostic significance discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
Potentially resectable. The four peripheral liver metastases (2‑3.5 cm) are within size limits and are not described as involving major vessels or biliary structures, and there is no extra‑hepatic disease. RAS‑wild‑type status is favorable. However, critical technical data (hepatic segments involved, vascular contact, future liver remnant volume, liver MRI) and the fact that the primary rectal tumor has not yet been resected make a definitive “resectable” classification premature; therefore the case is best considered potentially resectable pending conversion therapy and detailed anatomic assessment.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Initiate systemic conversion chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± cetuximab) for 2–3 months.  
   • Goal: downsize liver lesions, eradicate micrometastatic disease, and obtain a “biologic test” of tumor aggressiveness given the presence of circulating tumor cells.  

B. Restaging with high‑resolution liver MRI (gadoxetate‑enhanced) plus repeat thoraco‑abdominal CT; calculate future liver remnant (FLR) volume and assess vascular/biliary involvement.  
   • Provides precise mapping for surgical planning and determines whether portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy is required.  

C. If imaging confirms that an R0 liver resection can be achieved while preserving ≥20‑30 % FLR, proceed with a liver‑first (reverse) approach:  
   • Perform curative‑intent hepatic resection (single‑stage if FLR adequate; otherwise staged resection or PVE‑augmented resection).  
   • Aim for negative margins (R0) and preserve at least two contiguous hepatic segments.  

D. After hepatic recovery (6–8 weeks) address the primary rectal cancer:  
   • If not already given, deliver neoadjuvant chemoradiation (short‑course RT ± consolidation chemotherapy) followed by total mesorectal excision (TME) with appropriate sphincter‑preserving or APR technique based on tumor location and response.  
   • Post‑operative adjuvant systemic therapy (continuation of the same regimen or switch to maintenance) to complete a full peri‑operative treatment course.
Reference:

The patient presents with four peripheral liver metastases (2–3.5 cm) without reported extrahepatic disease. The lesions are limited in number and anatomically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is resectable. The presence of circulating tumor cells suggests higher systemic risk but does not alter technical resectability.

A. Preoperative staging and integration with rectal management
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define vascular and biliary relationships and calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Pelvic MRI to plan rectal treatment (chemoradiotherapy).

• The objective is treatment of micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Radiologic reassessment after treatment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 2-3 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Surgical management after restaging : management of the rectal primary (oncologic priority)
• Given the T3N2 rectal cancer, long-course radiotherapy is appropriate to optimize local control and allow coordinated surgical planning.

E. Coordinated surgical strategy
• Initiate doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX) during the waiting period following radiotherapy. This period treats potential micrometastatic disease and tests tumor biology.
• Consider either parenchymal-sparing wedge/segmentectomy or ablation if no biliary or large vessels proximity) aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvis MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor

• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.

Case_Content:
Woman, 68 years old, right T4N2 colon cancer, multiple liver metastases (≥10 lesions) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 2700 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Massive liver disease with high marker elevation, unfavorable prognosis.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline) – the disease is not clearly resectable because:  
  • ≥10 hepatic lesions (high tumor burden) makes a single‑stage R0 resection unlikely without compromising future liver remnant (FLR).  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease on CT (favors resectability).  
  • KRAS mutation and markedly elevated CEA (2700 ng/mL) indicate aggressive biology, supporting the need for down‑staging before surgery.  
- Rationale: Current hepatobiliary criteria require (a) ability to achieve R0 resection of all lesions, (b) preservation of at least two contiguous liver segments with adequate inflow/outflow, and (c) FLR ≥ 20‑30 % of total liver volume. With ≥10 lesions the technical feasibility is uncertain, but conversion therapy may render the disease resectable; therefore it is deemed “potentially resectable” pending response and further anatomic assessment.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Systemic conversion chemotherapy  
   - Initiate oxaliplatin‑based doublet (e.g., mFOLFOX6) combined with bevacizumab (KRAS‑mutated tumors are not candidates for anti‑EGFR agents).  
   - Goal: tumor shrinkage, reduction of lesion number/size, and assessment of disease biology.  

B. Radiologic reassessment (≈8‑10 weeks)  
   - Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast and repeat thoraco‑abdominal CT.  
   - Evaluate: maximum lesion diameter, segmental distribution, vascular/biliary involvement, and calculate FLR (volumetry).  

C. Decision point after imaging  
   - If sufficient tumor response (e.g., reduction to ≤4‑5 lesions, FLR ≥ 30 %): proceed to curative‑intent hepatic resection (single‑stage or staged according to distribution).  
   - If FLR remains inadequate but disease is otherwise resectable: consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy, followed by re‑assessment.  
   - If disease remains extensive or progresses: continue systemic therapy (possible switch to FOLFIRI + bevacizumab) or integrate locoregional therapies (e.g., hepatic arterial infusion, radio‑frequency ablation) as palliation.  

D. Management of the primary colon tumor  
   - If the primary has not yet been resected and is asymptomatic: schedule definitive right‑colectomy after hepatic disease is controlled (sequential “liver‑first” approach).  
   - If obstructive, perforated, or bleeding: perform urgent colectomy (simultaneous with liver resection only if hepatic disease is already resectable and patient fitness permits).  

E. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy  
   - After R0 liver resection (and primary resection if applicable), resume the same chemotherapy regimen for 6 months if tolerated, or consider maintenance bevacizumab alone.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with ≥10 liver metastases in the context of a right T4N2 colon cancer and very high CEA (2700 ng/mL). The tumor burden, multiplicity of lesions, and likely bilobar distribution preclude the possibility of achieving a complete R0 resection while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered unresectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships.
• Given the high CEA level (2700 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Systemic therapy as primary strategy (mandatory)
• Initiate intensive systemic chemotherapy according to MDT decision (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab; KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR).
• The objective is global disease control and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Radiologic reassessment after treatment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 3-6 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgery (exceptional)
• Surgical re-evaluation could be considered only in the rare situation of major radiologic and biologic response with significant reduction in number and size of lesions allowing parenchymal-sparing resections.

D. If disease remains extensive
• Continue second-line systemic therapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented management according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Man, 63 years old, left T3N1M1 colon cancer at the abdominal CT scan, three liver metastases (2-3 cm) and confirmed left portal invasion on liver MRI. CEA 310 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Unilateral portal involvement, potentially approachable depending on volume.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline resectable)  
- Rationale:  
   Three metastases, each ≤3 cm, satisfy size and number criteria for resection.  
   No documented extra‑hepatic disease on available imaging; thoracic CT has not been performed, so distant spread cannot be excluded.  
   MRI shows left portal vein invasion, indicating vascular involvement that may compromise a curative R0 resection without adjuncts.  
   Technical feasibility depends on future liver remnant (FLR) volume and ability to preserve at least two contiguous segments with adequate inflow/outflow; FLR data are missing.  
   Because portal invasion can often be managed with portal vein embolization (PVE) or a staged hepatectomy, the disease is not outright unresectable but requires conversion/optimization strategies.  

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy  
   - Administer 4–6 cycles of a fluoropyrimidine‑oxaliplatin doublet (FOLFOX) ± anti‑VEGF (bevacizumab) or anti‑EGFR depending on KRAS status (to be obtained).  
   - Goals: assess tumor biology, achieve possible downsizing of liver lesions, and treat microscopic portal invasion.  

B. Comprehensive restaging  
   - Perform contrast‑enhanced chest CT (or PET/CT) to exclude pulmonary metastases.  
   - Repeat liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to re‑evaluate lesion size, vascular involvement, and calculate FLR volume.  
   - Obtain CT‑based volumetry; if FLR <30 % (or <20 % in compromised liver), plan for portal vein embolization or two‑stage approach.  

C. Surgical sequencing (liver‑first approach)  
   - If FLR is adequate after chemotherapy (or after PVE‑induced hypertrophy), proceed with parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy targeting the left‑portal‑involved segment(s) while preserving ≥2 contiguous segments.  
   - Use intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm margins; aim for R0 resection.  
   - If FLR remains insufficient, schedule PVE of the involved lobe followed by interval (≈4–6 weeks) for hypertrophy, then complete resection (potential two‑stage hepatectomy).  

D. Management of the primary colon tumor  
   - After hepatic clearance and patient recovery (≈4–6 weeks), perform a left‑sided colectomy (segmental or left hemicolectomy) if the primary has not yet been resected.  
   - If the primary is asymptomatic and liver surgery is limited (minor resection), a simultaneous colon‑liver resection could be considered, but only after confirming patient fitness and adequate operative time.
Reference:

The patient presents with three liver metastases (2–3 cm) associated with confirmed left portal vein invasion on MRI, without reported extrahepatic disease. Although the number of lesions is limited, portal involvement compromises the feasibility of a safe R0 resection while preserving an adequate future liver remnant at this stage. • Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to confirm the relationship of the 3 lesions to vascular and biliary structures. Precise anatomical mapping is required to plan a safe parenchymal-sparing resection.
• Given the high CEA level (310 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

• The elevated CEA level (310 ng/mL) and multiplicity of lesions suggest biologically active disease.

• KRAS status is unknown
• This period treats micrometastatic disease and evaluates tumor biology.

• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and evaluate vascular/biliary relationships.

• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a first left hepatectomy with parenchymal-sparing liver resection of the remaining lesions aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins.

• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals given the elevated initial tumor marker (CEA 150 ng/mL).

Case_Content:
Woman, 72 years old, right T3N0M1 colon tumor, single 5.6 cm metastasis in segment VIII, in close contact with IVC at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 540 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Large central metastasis, major technical question regarding surgical approach.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Rationale:  
  • Single hepatic lesion (5.6 cm) in segment VIII – meets oncologic criterion of solitary disease amenable to R0 resection.  
  • No extra‑hepatic metastases identified on thoraco‑abdominal CT (pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal, bone disease assumed absent).  
  • RAS wild‑type supports use of effective conversion chemotherapy and potential for curative intent.  
  • Close contact with the inferior vena cava represents a technical limitation; invasion would require vascular reconstruction, which raises operative risk and may render the lesion unresectable without further assessment.  
  • Lack of data on future liver remnant (FLR) volume, hepatic inflow/outflow preservation, and liver function prevents a definitive “resectable” label.  
  • Therefore the case is best described as potentially resectable pending additional imaging, volumetry, and response to systemic therapy.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Diagnostic work‑up – Obtain a high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and 3‑D reconstruction; perform volumetric analysis to calculate FLR ratio; assess arterial, portal, and IVC anatomy; evaluate liver function (ICG clearance, bilirubin, AST/ALT, platelets) and patient performance status (ASA, cardiopulmonary reserve).  
B. Systemic conversion therapy – Initiate 2–3 months of intensive doublet or triplet chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI) combined with an anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) given RAS wild‑type, to (i) test tumor biology, (ii) potentially downsize the lesion, and (iii) treat occult micrometastases.  
C. Re‑assessment – Repeat MRI and volumetry after chemotherapy. If the lesion remains resectable with clear margins and FLR ≥ 30 % (or FLR/BW ≥ 0.5 %), proceed to hepatic surgery. If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage/ALPPS approach before definitive resection.  
D. Surgical sequence –  
   • Liver‑first (reverse) approach is preferred because the primary right‑colon tumor is asymptomatic (no obstruction, bleeding, or perforation reported) and the hepatic operation will likely be a major right hepatectomy or extended segmental resection with possible IVC reconstruction.  
   • Perform right hepatectomy or segment VIII non‑anatomical resection with negative margins; manage IVC involvement with vascular control and, if needed, patch repair or graft reconstruction.  
   • After hepatic recovery (typically 4–6 weeks), perform definitive right hemicolectomy (primary tumor resection).  
   • Complete peri‑operative systemic therapy (adjuvant chemotherapy) to a total of 6 months, adjusting based on pathological response and postoperative recovery.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single 5.6 cm liver metastasis in segment VIII in close contact with the IVC, without reported extrahepatic disease. Although solitary, the central location and caval proximity make a standard parenchymal-sparing R0 resection technically demanding and potentially unsafe without prior tumor downsizing or vascular planning. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable, but only after careful vascular assessment and likely induction therapy.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI to define exact segmental distribution of the lesion with detailed vascular and biliary relationships. 
• Given the high CEA level (540 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Intensive conversion systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Initiate 2–3 months of induction chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• The objective is significant tumor downsizing, reduction in number/volume of lesions, and clearance from the IVC to enable potential surgical planning.

C. Close radiologic monitoring
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2-3 months to assess response, particularly:
– Relationship of lesions to the IVC.
– Global reduction of liver tumor burden.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Monitor CEA kinetics as an indicator of treatment response.

D. Surgical management if feasibility is confirmed
• Repeat high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of the lesion to the IVC and hepatic veins.
• If regression occurs or vascular control is deemed feasible, plan an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resection of segment VIII, aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Anticipate possible IVC tangential resection or reconstruction with multidisciplinary discussion with vascular surgery to assess feasibility of tangential IVC resection if needed.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Management of primary tumor
• After recovery, perform right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon cancer) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. If insufficient response
• Continue systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.

G. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Case_Content:
Woman, 65 years old, T4N1M1 rectal tumor, four liver metastases at the abdominal CT scan, CEA 60 ng/mL, RAS wild-type, MSI-H.
MDT Discussion: Immuno-sensitive profile, discussion on optimal therapeutic sequence.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
The patient is classified as potentially resectable.  
- Four hepatic lesions do not preclude curative intent if they can be cleared with negative margins and an adequate future liver remnant (FLR ≥ 30 % in a normal liver).  
- No data are provided on lesion size, segmental distribution, proximity to major vessels or biliary structures, or calculated FLR; these technical factors are essential to confirm outright resectability.  
- The primary rectal tumor is T4, indicating locally advanced disease that typically requires neoadjuvant chemoradiation before any definitive resection; this influences the sequencing but not the intrinsic hepatic resectability.  
- No extra‑hepatic disease has been documented, but chest imaging and peritoneal assessment are missing; the presence of limited extra‑hepatic disease could still allow a combined curative approach.  
- Molecular profile (RAS‑wt, MSI‑H) suggests favorable response to immunotherapy, supporting a neoadjuvant systemic strategy that may down‑size liver lesions and improve resectability.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging – obtain high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast, pelvic MRI for the rectal primary, and chest CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out occult extra‑hepatic disease; calculate FLR using volumetry and assess vascular anatomy.  
B. Systemic induction therapy – start pembrolizumab (or pembrolizumab + chemotherapy per current MSI‑H guidelines) to exploit the immunogenic phenotype and potentially shrink hepatic lesions.  
C. Neoadjuvant chemoradiation for the rectal primary – deliver long‑course chemoradiotherapy (or short‑course RT followed by systemic therapy) to achieve maximal down‑staging of the T4 lesion before any abdominal surgery.  
D. Re‑assessment after systemic/locoregional therapy – repeat liver MRI and pelvic MRI; if hepatic disease is now technically resectable with an adequate FLR, proceed to a liver‑first (reverse) approach:  
   - If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization or a two‑stage hepatectomy.  
   - Perform curative liver resection (anatomical or parenchymal‑sparing) aiming for R0 margins.  
E. Definitive rectal surgery – after hepatic clearance and adequate recovery (typically 6–8 weeks), perform total mesorectal excision (TME) with appropriate sphincter‑preserving or abdominoperineal resection based on tumor response.  
F. Adjuvant therapy – consider postoperative systemic therapy (e.g., continuation of immunotherapy) based on final pathology and response.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four liver metastases in the setting of a T4N1 rectal tumor. Although the liver disease may be technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resection, the MSI-H profile indicates a high likelihood of major response to immunotherapy. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is potentially resectable, but surgery is not the first step given the expected efficacy of systemic immunotherapy.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to confirm the relationship of the 4 lesions to vascular and biliary structures. Precise anatomical mapping is required to plan a safe parenchymal-sparing resection.

B. First-line systemic immunotherapy (mandatory)
• Initiate immunotherapy according to MDT decision as first-line treatment for MSI-H metastatic colorectal cancer.
• The objective is major tumor regression and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 2–3 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Surgical re-evaluation after response
• If a major radiologic response occurs, reassess segmental resectability.
• Plan biopsy of the primary rectal tumor and liver metastases to assess tumor response to immunotherapy
• Consider parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided liver resections only if residual lesions persist and complete clearance is feasible with adequate future liver remnant.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic immunotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals

Case_Content:
Man, 60 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer, eight bilobar liver metastases at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 1300 ng/mL, KRAS mutated. Liver MRI: contact with right hepatic vein.
MDT Discussion: Superior vascular invasion, significant operative risk.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Current classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
- Rationale:  
   Technical factors – eight bilobar metastases, contact with the right hepatic vein (vascular involvement) and no reported FLR data make an immediate R0 resection unsafe.  
   Biological factors – T4 primary, N2 nodal disease, KRAS mutation, very high CEA (1300 ng/mL) indicate aggressive biology and higher recurrence risk.  
   Operative risk – MDT notes “significant operative risk” and “superior vascular invasion,” supporting the need for down‑staging before attempting major hepatectomy.  
   No extra‑hepatic disease is identified, so the only barrier is hepatic tumor burden and vascular involvement, which can be addressed with conversion therapy and/or staged surgical approaches (PVE, two‑stage hepatectomy, ALPPS).  

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Systemic conversion chemotherapy  
   - Initiate an oxaliplatin‑based regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI) combined with bevacizumab (anti‑VEGF) because KRAS is mutated and anti‑EGFR agents are ineffective.  
   - Goal: achieve ≥30 % reduction in total tumor volume and, if possible, convert vascular contact to a resectable margin.  

B. Re‑assessment after 3–4 cycles  
   - Repeat triphasic CT and liver‑specific MRI with volumetry to determine:  
     • Residual disease distribution, size of each lesion, and status of right hepatic vein involvement.  
     • Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio; aim for ≥30 % (≥40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is suspected).  
   - Multidisciplinary review to decide between: (i) single‑stage resection, (ii) portal vein embolization (PVE) followed by right hepatectomy, or (iii) two‑stage hepatectomy (left lateral segment first, then right).  

C. Surgical phase (if down‑staging successful)  
   - If FLR adequate after down‑staging: proceed to an R0 right hepatectomy with vascular reconstruction as needed (e.g., patch repair of hepatic vein).  
   - If FLR insufficient: perform right PVE (or ALPPS if rapid hypertrophy required) and re‑image after 2–4 weeks; once FLR meets criteria, complete right hepatectomy.  
   - Intra‑operative ultrasound to detect occult lesions; aim for ≥1 cm margin when feasible.  

D. Management of the primary colon tumor  
   - If the primary has not yet been resected, schedule colectomy after hepatic resection once the patient has recovered, or consider simultaneous resection only if the hepatic procedure is limited (e.g., left lateral segmentectomy) and the patient’s physiologic reserve permits.  
   - Pathologic staging of the primary (grade, lymphovascular invasion) will further inform adjuvant therapy.  

E. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy  
   - Post‑operative systemic therapy (continuation of the same regimen or switch to FOLFIRI + bevacizumab) for at least 6 months, tailored to response and tolerance.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with eight bilobar liver metastases with MRI showing contact with the right hepatic vein, in the context of a right T4N2 colon cancer and markedly elevated CEA (1300 ng/mL). The tumor burden, bilobar distribution, and venous contact make a safe R0 resection with preservation of adequate venous outflow and future liver remnant not achievable at this stage. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered unresectable upfront.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence

Case_Content:
Woman, 55 years old, left colon cancer, multiple bilobar metastases at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 2100 ng/mL, BRAF wild-type, HER2 amplified.
MDT Discussion: Particular molecular profile, possible sensitivity to an anti-HER2 approach.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
The patient cannot be definitively classified as resectable, potentially resectable, or unresectable with the data provided. Bilobar disease on CT suggests a technically challenging situation that may be convertible to resectability if an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved and no major vascular or biliary invasion is present. However, the absence of critical information (number and size of lesions, segmental distribution, FLR calculation, vascular contact, performance status, and presence of occult extra‑hepatic disease) precludes a reliable classification. Consequently, the disease is best regarded as potentially resectable pending further work‑up.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Systemic therapy (induction)  
   • Initiate HER2‑directed doublet (e.g., trastuzumab + pertuzumab) combined with a standard doublet chemotherapy backbone (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI) because the tumor is HER2‑amplified and BRAF wild‑type.  
   • Rationale: high CEA (2100 ng/mL) indicates biologically aggressive disease; targeted therapy may achieve tumor shrinkage and provide an early “proof of time” to assess tumor biology.  

B. Comprehensive restaging after 2–3 months of induction  
   • Obtain contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast, repeat multiphase abdominal CT, and a thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) to evaluate pulmonary, bone, and brain sites.  
   • Re‑calculate FLR using volumetric software; if FLR < 30 % (or < 20 % in steatotic liver), consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy.  
   • Rationale: precise anatomic mapping and FLR assessment are mandatory before any hepatic resection.  

C. Re‑assessment of resectability (multidisciplinary)  
   • If imaging shows sufficient FLR and all liver lesions are amenable to R0 resection (with ≤ 1 cm margins), proceed to curative‑intent hepatic surgery.  
   • If disease remains extensive but down‑staged, consider a staged approach (PVE → resection or ALPPS) or add local ablative modalities (thermal ablation or SBRT) for lesions in difficult locations.  
   • Rationale: conversion strategies aim to achieve complete clearance while preserving liver function.  

D. Management of the primary colorectal tumor  
   • If the primary lesion is asymptomatic and has not yet been resected, adopt a “liver‑first” sequence: complete hepatic surgery first, then perform definitive colorectal resection (low anterior resection or segmental colectomy) after postoperative recovery.  
   • If the primary is symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding, perforation), address it urgently (stenting, diversion, or resection) before or concurrently with liver surgery.  
   • Rationale: controlling the dominant disease burden first (liver) improves overall survival when the primary is not causing acute complications.  

E. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy  
   • After R0 liver resection (and primary resection), resume HER2‑targeted therapy ± chemotherapy for a total of 6–12 months, based on response and tolerance.  
   • Enroll the patient in a clinical trial of HER2‑directed therapy in the peri‑operative setting if available.  
   • Rationale: continuation of effective systemic therapy reduces the risk of early recurrence, which is high in patients with high baseline CEA.
Reference:

The patient presents with multiple bilobar liver metastases and very high CEA (2100 ng/mL) in the context of a left colon cancer with HER2 amplification and BRAF wild-type status. • HER2-positive colorectal cancer (CRC), found in 2–6% of cases (mainly RAS wild-type and left-sided), is treated with targeted therapies like trastuzumab combined with tucatinib or trastuzumab deruxtecan.

• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 2–3 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Surgical management after restaging
• If disease remains controlled, perform ultrasound-guided left lateral sectoriectomy (rection of segments II and III) aiming for R0 margins.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

• After recovery, perform left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.

Case_Content:
Man, 62 years old, T3N1M1 upper rectal tumor, liver metastases (3-5 cm) with contact with IVC and right hepatic vein at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 580 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Complex central metastases, discussion on combined approach or venous reconstruction.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (requires further evaluation).  
- Justification:  
  • Liver lesions are 3–5 cm and demonstrate contact with the inferior vena cava and the right hepatic vein, indicating possible major vascular involvement that may necessitate venous reconstruction.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease is identified on current imaging.  
  • The future liver remnant (FLR) volume, number of lesions, exact segmental distribution, and arterial/portal anatomy are not provided; these are essential to determine whether an R0 resection with adequate hepatic reserve is feasible.  
  • Absence of data on response to systemic therapy prevents confirmation that disease is biologically controlled.  
  • Given the vascular contact but without documented invasion, a curative‑intent hepatectomy with vascular reconstruction or a staged approach remains possible if FLR is sufficient and systemic disease is controlled.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Systemic induction therapy – Start a doublet chemotherapy regimen (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) ± biologic agent based on molecular profile. Rationale: to down‑size liver lesions, assess tumor biology, and increase the chance of achieving an R0 resection while also treating occult micrometastatic disease.  
B. Concurrent rectal neoadjuvant treatment – Deliver long‑course chemoradiotherapy (or short‑course RT followed by chemotherapy) for the upper‑rectal primary. Rationale: to achieve maximal down‑staging of the primary, reduce risk of local recurrence, and allow a safer subsequent colorectal resection.  
C. Restaging imaging – Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with liver‑specific contrast and repeat thoraco‑abdominal CT after 2–3 months of systemic therapy. Include volumetric analysis to calculate FLR and detailed vascular mapping. Rationale: to confirm resectability, evaluate response, and plan need for portal vein embolization (PVE) or venous reconstruction.  
D. Surgical sequencing (liver‑first approach) –  
   1. If FLR ≥30 % (or ≥40 % in steatotic liver) and vascular reconstruction is feasible, proceed with hepatectomy (right or extended right hepatectomy) with IVC/right hepatic vein reconstruction as required.  
   2. If FLR is insufficient, perform PVE (or ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy, then complete hepatic resection after adequate growth.  
   3. After hepatic surgery and recovery, perform total mesorectal excision (TME) of the rectal cancer, timing dictated by wound healing and patient performance status.  
   Rationale: addressing the liver first prevents loss of resectability due to progression while the rectal tumor is being down‑staged; it also allows a major hepatic operation without the added morbidity of a simultaneous low anterior resection.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with centrally located liver metastases (3–5 cm) in contact with the IVC and the right hepatic vein in the setting of an upper rectal T3N1 tumor, without reported extrahepatic disease. Although the number of lesions is not specified as excessive, the venous involvement makes a standard parenchymal-sparing R0 resection unsafe without complex vascular control or reconstruction. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable only after tumor downsizing and expert HPB / vascular reassessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver and pelvis MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships.
• Given the high CEA level (580 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Mandatory induction systemic therapy
• Initiate 2–3 months of induction chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).
• The objective is tumor downsizing and reduction of venous contact.

• Repeat high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of lesions to the IVC and right hepatic vein.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Multidisciplinary evaluation with complex surgery to assess feasibility of venous reconstruction if required or right hepatomy including en-bloc resection of the right hepatic vein according to the future liver remnant.

D. Surgical management if feasibility is confirmed
• If regression occurs or venous reconstruction is deemed feasible, plan an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resection with the aim of R0 margin.
• Anticipate possible IVC and/or hepatic vein reconstruction.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.

E. Surgical management after restaging : management of the rectal primary (oncologic priority)
• Given the T3N1 rectal cancer, long-course radiotherapy is appropriate to optimize local control and allow coordinated surgical planning.
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvis MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : with strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery, using a staged or synchronous strategy : oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

F. If disease remains extensive
• Continue systemic and targeted therapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented management according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Woman, 67 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer, multiple liver metastases at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan and normal CEA at 3 ng/mL. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Biological discordance, question regarding the utility of CEA follow-up in this profile.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
- Rationale:  
  • Advanced primary (right‑sided T4N2) and KRAS mutation are adverse biologic factors that lower the likelihood of cure with surgery alone.  
  • Imaging shows “multiple liver metastases” but no details on number, size, segmental distribution, vascular or biliary involvement, or future liver remnant (FLR) volume; therefore technical resectability cannot be confirmed.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease is documented (pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal assumed absent), which does not preclude liver resection if hepatic disease can be cleared.  
  • Performance status, comorbidities, liver function, and prior systemic therapy are unknown; these medical factors are required to deem a patient fit for major hepatectomy.  
  • Given the uncertainty, the case fits the “borderline” category where neoadjuvant systemic therapy is usually employed to achieve down‑staging and to obtain a “proof of time” before committing to surgery.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Initial systemic therapy (neoadjuvant)  
   – Initiate an intensive doublet or triplet chemotherapy regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI) combined with anti‑VEGF (bevacizumab) because the disease is KRAS‑mutated and biologically aggressive.  
   – Goal: tumor shrinkage, assessment of disease biology, and preservation of future liver remnant.  

B. Restaging after 2–3 months  
   – Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast (or contrast‑enhanced CT if MRI unavailable) to define number, size, segmental involvement, vascular contact, and calculate FLR.  
   – Re‑evaluate performance status, liver function (bilirubin, INR, platelets), and obtain CA 19‑9 (if not already measured) for prognostic information.  

C. Surgical planning  
   – If restaging shows that an R0 resection is technically feasible with an FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 20 % after portal vein embolization), proceed with a liver‑first (reverse) approach because the primary tumor is asymptomatic and the hepatic burden appears dominant.  
   – Perform an anatomic or parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy (potentially staged or combined with portal vein embolization) to achieve negative margins.  

D. Management of the primary colon cancer  
   – After hepatic resection and recovery, undertake curative resection of the right colon primary (segmental colectomy with adequate lymphadenectomy).  
   – Follow with adjuvant systemic therapy (same regimen as neoadjuvant, adjusted for postoperative tolerance) to address micrometastatic disease.

Case_Content:
Man, 58 years old, left T3N1M1 colon cancer, bilobar metastases (1.5-3 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 400 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, POLE mutation detected.
MDT Discussion: Hypermutated profile, rare, may justify immunotherapy in some strategies.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
- Rationale: Bilobar disease with lesions 1.5‑3 cm is technically amenable to curative‑intent surgery provided an adequate future liver remnant (FLR ≥ 30 % in a normal liver) can be preserved and no major vascular or biliary invasion is present. The absence of documented FLR, vascular contact, exact lesion count, and hepatic segment distribution precludes a definitive “resectable” label; therefore the case is placed in the potentially resectable category pending further anatomic and functional assessment.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Complete staging work‑up  
   - Perform liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast to define lesion number, segmental distribution, vascular/biliary involvement, and to calculate FLR volume.  
   - Obtain PET‑CT (or confirm existing thoraco‑abdominal CT) to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease (especially brain, bone, peritoneum).  
   - Assess performance status (ECOG), comorbidities (Charlson index), liver function tests, and baseline cardiopulmonary fitness.  

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy  
   - Initiate an oxaliplatin‑based doublet (e.g., FOLFOX) combined with an anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab) given RAS‑wild type status.  
   - Because the tumor harbors a POLE mutation (hyper‑mutated phenotype), evaluate microsatellite instability (MSI) / mismatch repair status; if MSI‑high or high TMB, consider adding a checkpoint inhibitor (pembrolizumab) either concurrently or sequentially.  
   - Plan for 3–4 cycles, then re‑image to assess radiologic response and biological response (CEA trend).  

C. Re‑assessment of resectability  
   - After systemic therapy, repeat MRI and volumetry.  
   - If FLR remains insufficient, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy (including possible associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy – ALPPS) to augment FLR.  
   - If disease is down‑staged to a resectable burden with clear margins achievable, proceed with a liver‑first approach (resection of liver metastases before primary colon tumor) because the primary is asymptomatic (no obstruction, perforation, or bleeding reported).  

D. Surgical phase  
   - Perform curative‑intent liver resection (anatomical or parenchymal‑sparing) aiming for R0 margins; use intra‑operative ultrasound to guide.  
   - After hepatic recovery (typically 4–6 weeks), address the primary left‑sided colon cancer with segmental colectomy (or extended resection if required). If intra‑operative assessment shows the primary is easily resectable and patient condition permits, a simultaneous colon‑liver resection can be considered.  

E. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy  
   - Continue postoperative systemic therapy (same regimen as neoadjuvant) for 3–6 months, adjusting based on pathology (margin status, lymph‑node involvement).  
   - If POLE‑mutated tumor is confirmed MSI‑high, transition to immunotherapy maintenance per current guidelines.

• Plan ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resections only if complete clearance is feasible with adequate future liver remnant.

• Perform left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis

• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

• Complete a total of approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.

Case_Content:
Woman, 69 years old, T4N2M1 transverse colon cancer, seven liver metastases at the abdominal CT scan, CEA 1150 ng/mL, NRAS Q61R mutation.
MDT Discussion: Specific NRAS molecular profile, no sensitivity to anti-EGFR.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Justification:  
  • Seven hepatic lesions exceed the conventional “resectable” limit of ≤3–4 metastases.  
  • No data on individual lesion size, segmental distribution, or vascular/biliary involvement; these factors could further limit a one‑stage resection.  
  • Future liver remnant (FLR) volume is unknown; without confirmation that FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % after chemotherapy‑induced liver injury) a curative hepatectomy cannot be declared feasible.  
  • Primary colorectal tumor has not been resected; synchronous disease generally favors initial systemic therapy and/or staged colorectal resection.  
  • Extra‑hepatic disease has not been ruled out (thoracic CT, PET‑CT, bone/brain imaging missing). Presence of distant metastases would shift the case to “initially unresectable” unless they are limited and amenable to curative treatment.  
  • High CEA (1150 ng/mL) and NRAS Q61R mutation indicate aggressive biology, supporting a conversion‑therapy approach before surgery.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging  
   - Obtain high‑resolution thoraco‑abdominal CT or PET‑CT to exclude pulmonary, osseous, or cerebral metastases.  
   - Perform liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast (or contrast‑enhanced CT with thin cuts) to define lesion size, number, segmental involvement, and relationship to major vessels/bile ducts.  
   - Calculate FLR using volumetric software; consider functional assessment (e.g., indocyanine‑green clearance).  

B. Conversion systemic therapy  
   - Initiate intensive chemotherapy regimen appropriate for RAS‑mutated disease, e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab or mFOLFOX6 + bevacizumab, aiming for ≥ 30 % radiologic response.  
   - Monitor tumor markers (CEA) and radiologic response every 2–3 cycles.  

C. Re‑assessment and liver‑directed optimization  
   - After 2–3 months (or after 6 cycles) repeat liver MRI/CT to evaluate tumor shrinkage and FLR adequacy.  
   - If FLR remains insufficient but disease is down‑staged, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy (including possible associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy – ALPPS) to increase remnant volume.  

D. Surgical phase  
   - If hepatic disease becomes resectable: plan curative‑intent liver resection with intent of R0 margins; use intra‑operative ultrasound to detect occult lesions.  
   - Primary tumor management:  
        • If the primary is asymptomatic and patient’s condition permits, perform simultaneous colorectal resection (segmental colectomy) with liver surgery.  
        • If the primary is symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding) or patient’s physiologic reserve is limited, defer colorectal resection to a second‑stage operation after hepatic recovery.  
   - Post‑operative: resume/adapt systemic therapy (adjuvant or continuation) for at least 6 months, tailored to response and tolerability.

• If symptomatic or if consideration of intra arterial chemotherapy, perform extended right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right and transverse colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.

Case_Content:
Man, 70 years old, left colon tumor, three liver metastases at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 200 ng/mL, RAS wild-type, MSS. MRI: invasion of the hepatic vein confluence.
MDT Discussion: Superior vascular involvement, significant technical risk, volume to be assessed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Justification:  
  • Three synchronous liver metastases – number alone does not preclude resection.  
  • MRI demonstrates invasion of the hepatic vein confluence, indicating major vascular involvement that raises technical difficulty and risk of inadequate outflow.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease identified on thoraco‑abdominal CT.  
  • Adequate future liver remnant (FLR) has not been quantified; without volumetric data the case cannot be declared technically resectable.  
  • Because vascular reconstruction or hypertrophy strategies (PVE/ALPPS) may be required, the disease is considered borderline/potentially resectable pending further assessment.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Systemic induction therapy  
   – Administer an intensive doublet or triplet regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± anti‑EGFR antibody) given RAS‑wild‑type status.  
   – Goal: assess tumor biology (“proof of time”), achieve possible downsizing of hepatic lesions, and treat occult micrometastatic disease.  

B. Restaging and functional assessment (4–6 weeks after induction)  
   – Repeat high‑quality liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and CT‑based volumetry to:  
        • Measure maximum lesion diameters, segmental distribution, and relationship to portal/hepatic arterial structures.  
        • Calculate FLR ratio (target ≥ 30 % in a normal liver, ≥ 40 % if prior chemotherapy or steatosis).  
   – Evaluate liver function (bilirubin, INR, albumin, ICG clearance if available) and patient performance status.  

C. Decision point based on restaging  
   • If FLR adequate and vascular invasion amenable to resection – proceed to definitive hepatic surgery with en‑bloc resection of the involved hepatic vein confluence and reconstruction (e.g., interpositional graft or patch).  
   • If FLR insufficient – schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) of the liver sector to be resected, or consider ALPPS/2‑stage hepatectomy, re‑image after 2–3 weeks to confirm hypertrophy.  
   • If disease progression – continue systemic therapy or consider alternative local therapies (radiofrequency ablation, stereotactic body radiotherapy) and reassess resectability later.  

D. Primary colorectal tumor management  
   – If the primary has not yet been resected and is asymptomatic, adopt a liver‑first approach after induction therapy, reserving primary resection for a second operation once hepatic clearance is achieved.  
   – If the primary is symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding, perforation) or high‑risk, perform simultaneous resection after confirming that hepatic surgery will remain safe (e.g., limited hepatectomy with adequate FLR).  

E. Post‑operative adjuvant therapy and surveillance  
   – Resume or complete systemic chemotherapy (total 6 months peri‑operative preferred).  
   – Serial CEA monitoring and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–4 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months up to 5 years.

The patient presents with three liver metastases and MRI evidence of invasion of the hepatic vein confluence, without reported extrahepatic disease. Although the number of lesions is limited, involvement of the venous outflow confluence makes a safe R0 resection with preservation of adequate hepatic venous drainage technically uncertain at this stage. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable only after tumor downsizing and expert vascular reassessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships of all lesions.
• Given the high CEA level (200 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Mandatory induction systemic therapy
• Initiate 2–3 months of induction chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• The objective is tumor downsizing and potential reduction of venous involvement.

C. Radiologic reassessment after treatment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 2-3 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Expert HPB/vascular and volumetric restaging
• Repeat high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of lesions to the hepatic vein confluence.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR) and evaluate feasibility of venous preservation or need for reconstruction.

E. Surgical management if feasibility is confirmed
• If significant regression occurs, plan an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resection with the aim of R0 margin.
• Anticipate possible venous reconstruction or complex vascular control.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.

F. Management of primary tumor
• If symptomatic or if consideration of intra arterial chemotherapy, perform left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

G. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Case_Content:
Woman, 56 years old, right T3N1M1 colon cancer, four liver metastases (3-5 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 780 ng/mL, non-V600E BRAF mutation (D594G).
MDT Discussion: Atypical BRAF mutation, intermediate prognosis, bilobar liver involvement.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Rationale:  
  • Four liver metastases ranging 3‑5 cm in a bilobar distribution meet technical criteria for resection only if an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved; FLR data are missing.  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease, but high CEA (780 ng/mL) and a non‑V600E BRAF mutation (D594G) indicate aggressive biology, favoring neoadjuvant systemic therapy before definitive surgery.  
  • Absence of information on vascular or biliary involvement, hepatic segmental location, and liver function precludes an “upfront resectable” designation.  

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Induction systemic therapy  
   – Initiate intensive chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI) combined with bevacizumab; consider adding a BRAF‑directed regimen if a trial is available, recognizing D594G is not a V600E target.  
   – Objective: tumor down‑staging, assessment of disease biology, and potential FLR hypertrophy (via portal vein embolization if indicated).  

B. Restaging and functional assessment  
   – Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast and repeat thoraco‑abdominal CT.  
   – Calculate FLR volume; aim for ≥30 % (≥40 % if underlying liver compromise).  
   – Re‑evaluate CEA trend and assess for any new extra‑hepatic lesions.  

C. Surgical planning  
   – If FLR is adequate and disease responds (partial response or stable disease), proceed to curative‑intent liver resection.  
   – Preferred approach: staged “liver‑first” or two‑stage hepatectomy (including portal vein embolization or ALPPS) depending on FLR adequacy and segmental distribution.  
   – If the primary colon tumor remains unresected and is asymptomatic, it can be addressed either simultaneously (if safe) or after hepatic surgery.  

D. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy  
   – Complete a total of 6 months of peri‑operative systemic therapy (including postoperative cycles).  
   – Consider enrollment in a clinical trial targeting BRAF‑mutant mCRC or maintenance bevacizumab.  
   – Schedule regular CEA monitoring and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–6 months for the first two years.

Case_Content:
Man, 65 years old, left T4N2M1 colon cancer, six liver metastases (2-4 cm)at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 320 ng/mL, RAS wild-type, MSS. Positive circulating tumor cells detected.
MDT Discussion: Presence of circulating tumor cells despite no visible extension, prognostic value discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Current classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
- Rationale:  
  • Six liver metastases (2–4 cm) exceed the traditional “≤4 lesions” cut‑off but each lesion is ≤5 cm, which, according to modern criteria, does not automatically preclude resection if an R0 margin and adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be achieved.  
  • No imaging data on hepatic segment distribution, vascular or biliary involvement, or FLR volume; these technical factors are essential to confirm true resectability.  
  • Primary colon cancer is T4N2 and has not been reported as resected; the primary must be controlled before or concurrently with hepatic surgery.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease identified on CT (lungs, peritoneum, nodes assumed negative), but brain imaging is missing.  
  • High CEA (320 ng/mL) and positive circulating tumor cells suggest aggressive biology, supporting a neoadjuvant (conversion) approach rather than immediate surgery.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Systemic conversion chemotherapy  
   – Initiate an oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX) combined with anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab) because the tumor is RAS‑wild‑type.  
   – Aim for 3–4 cycles, then reassess radiologically (CT ± gadolinium‑EOB MRI).  

B. Comprehensive restaging  
   – Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to define lesion number, segmental distribution, vascular/biliary proximity, and calculate FLR.  
   – Obtain PET‑CT or brain MRI to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease.  

C. Evaluation of primary tumor  
   – If the primary lesion is symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding, perforation) or at high risk, schedule either simultaneous resection with liver surgery (if technically feasible) or staged resection after hepatic disease control.  

D. Surgical planning  
   – If post‑chemotherapy imaging shows sufficient tumor shrinkage and FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % in compromised livers), proceed to curative‑intent hepatectomy aiming for R0 margins.  
   – For borderline FLR, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy (TSH) to induce hypertrophy before definitive resection.  
   – Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm resectability and guide any adjunctive ablative techniques for lesions that become marginally resectable.  

E. Adjuvant therapy  
   – After complete (R0) resection of liver and primary tumor, resume the same systemic regimen (or switch to FOLFIRI if progression) for 4–6 months as adjuvant treatment.
